entry.title: Boulder: October 22, 2026 City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Most discussed: Wildfire, Emergency management, Zoning, Budget, Open space, Bikes & pedestrians

  • Bike Security and Theft Reduction Update: Staff from Transportation and Mobility and the Boulder Police Department presented completed work on the council priority to reduce bike theft and improve bike security. Bike theft fell 14% year-over-year in 2026 and recovery rose 13%, with the team expecting to meet its 10% goals. Actions included Bike Index registration events, locking education, bike rack upgrades, and targeted bait-bike operations. Council members asked about data gaps, staffing constraints, e-bike theft, and encouraging bike shops to register bikes at sale. Remaining tasks include a long-term bike parking resource and downtown station signage.
  • Enhancing Boulder's Wildfire Resilience: Staff presented the Wildfire Ready 2030 framework, organized into four strategies and 25 programs with 10 tier-one priorities, supported by a Wildland Urban Interface Risk Index that ranks 12 western sections. They also introduced a Wildfire Ready Action Hub for residents, 14 performance measures, and roughly $10 million in current tier-one investment. Staff proposed about $1.85 million in 2027 enhancements from grants and an open space fund realignment. Council members pressed for more aggressive hardening targets, a mandatory hardening ordinance, contractor quality standards, evacuation and cell-coverage planning, and reconciling wildfire building standards.

entry.title: Boulder: October 1, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Meeting (Regular Meeting with Public Hearing on 2027 Budget)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Budget, Wildfire, Public comment, Council governance, Taxes & fees, Housing

  • Amend agenda and open comment: Council voted to add item 8A on the front range passenger rail sales tax measure to the agenda. Elisha reviewed the public participation guidelines and rules of decorum for open comment. Nineteen people signed up to speak with two-minute limits.
  • Open comment on federal, housing, tenant, and development concerns: Residents spoke on a range of issues including a request for council to respond to federal actions, tenant union formation, Boulderthon road closures, unpermitted small cell towers near Boulder Meadows, Belmont property hazards, and CU South and Gunbarrel parks and safety. Speakers also raised concerns about Spruce Pool, a proposed botanic garden at Hogan Pancost, and the East Boulder Rec Center. Staff and council responded to several comments.
  • Consent agenda: Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3H unanimously after a motion and second with no questions raised.
  • Call-up check-in for Nuropa campus site review: Council reviewed a site review application to redevelop the Nuropa campus with about 135 residential units and a height modification to four stories and 55 feet. Council Member Winer raised shadow and setback concerns, and the applicant responded that setbacks exceed 40 feet and solar analysis met city standards. No member called the item up.
  • Public hearing on 2027 recommended budget and ordinances: Staff presented the 2027 recommended budget totaling about 552.6 million, with a 2.35 percent operating budget increase and a 135.4 million capital budget. Highlights included wildfire funding of about 10.9 million, three new police lieutenants, affordable housing investments, and a proposed Spruce Pool operations reduction. Council discussed wildfire funding timing ahead of the October 22 study session and the relationship to open space funds.
  • Council proposals to hold or realign wildfire funding: Council Member Benjamin proposed holding about 2.5 million for wildfire mitigation, while Council Member Kaplan proposed holding 600,000. Staff noted the funding source would need to be identified and that realignment could occur through the adjustment-to-base process. Straw polls did not reach a majority, so the budget proceeded without these changes and council planned to revisit wildfire funding after the October 22 study session.
  • Council proposal to reallocate police funds to behavioral health response: Council Member Tisha proposed redirecting part of police funding toward partnerships for mental health and behavioral response to non-emergency calls. Housing and Human Services staff explained that the care program was restructured because of low call volumes and would relaunch with clinicians and case managers. Council Member Tisha withdrew the amendment after the explanation.
  • Adoption of 2027 budget ordinances: Council voted on four ordinances: adopting the 2027 budget (7-1 with Adams opposed), setting property mill levies for 2026 (unanimous), appropriating funds for 2027 (unanimous), and amending fees and taxes in the Boulder Revised Code (7-1 with Adams opposed). Several members made closing remarks about budget process, staff work, and the need for a longer-term budget cycle.
  • Straw poll supporting Front Range passenger rail sales tax measure: Council Member Winer asked council whether to take a position of support on the Front Range passenger rail sales tax measure. The straw poll was unanimous, directing staff to prepare a resolution of support for a future business meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: September 24, 2026 City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Most discussed: Police, Regional & state relations, Council governance, Crime & justice, Arts, culture & libraries, Homelessness

  • Opening remarks on Boulder Valley School District resilient school plan and city property interest: Council Member Benjamin noted BVSD passed a resilient school plan and asked city staff about discussions on possible city uses of district properties. City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermyde said the city is discussing with the district possible uses such as a police substation or training center, and will return to council with any proposals.
  • Public safety update: police staffing, public safety information center, and crime trends: Police Chief Steve Redford reported the department is authorized for 190 sworn officers and is currently 12 short, with about 30 unavailable for solo deployment. Dispatcher and records staffing were also discussed. Redford highlighted the new Public Safety Information Center, rising proactive policing, declining property crime, and rising assaults, along with drug, financial crime, and officer assault examples.
  • Council questions on police staffing, Flock-style camera integration, retention, e-bikes, and care team: Council asked about the Boulder Community Connect program integrating private cameras into the public safety center, retention strategies including facilities and cost of living, drug enforcement limits, the CARE team changes, and e-moto or e-bike enforcement. Staff explained that camera sharing is voluntary and that many departing officers cite housing costs and facilities. Requests for disaggregated race data and care team outcomes were made.
  • Police oversight: complaint classification, demographics, panel activities, and five-year review: Independent Police Monitor Sherri Dean presented 2025 complaint data, including 149 allegations and 18 sustained findings, along with demographic breakdowns and panel turnover. Panel co-chairs Lizzy Friend and Bill De La Cruz raised concerns that new intake gateways have reduced cases reaching the panel. A five-year review of the oversight system is underway, with a report expected in October.
  • Municipal court data on unhoused defendants, community court, and young adult cases: Presiding Judge Jeff Khan and Court Administrator Devon Kiss-Kelly reviewed municipal court data showing citations to unhoused defendants, the community court diversion program with hundreds of dismissals, and warrant and in-custody trends. They also covered young adult cases such as MIP, nuisance parties, noise, and fraudulent ID, with increasing large amplified party concerns on the Hill and coordination with CU.
  • Sister cities program resolution update: Assistant City Manager Pam Davis and City Clerk staff presented proposed updates to Resolution 631 to clarify application, review, annual reporting, and deactivation processes for sister city alliances. Staff recommended an online application, clear review timelines, deadlines for council consideration, standardized agreements, and a possible cap or formal deactivation process. Council generally supported a council committee to oversee the program, a possible cap, and an escalating compliance process.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Regular Meeting - September 17, 2026
entry.content:
Most discussed: Historic preservation, Regional & state relations, Housing, Development projects, Open space, Climate & sustainability

  • Roll Call and Open Comment Guidelines: The meeting was called to order and a roll call confirmed a quorum. Staff reviewed public participation guidelines covering decorum, sign-up requirements, audio-only testimony, and limits on remarks to city business. Twenty speakers had signed up, each allotted two minutes.
  • Panka Place Vacation and Fraser Meadows Expansion Comments: Multiple speakers from Fraser Meadows and neighboring areas spoke in favor of vacating Panka Place to create a safer shared street that keeps vehicle, emergency, and delivery access. Supporters cited lack of city maintenance, improved walkability, and preserving the church's presence. The project is intended to support senior housing expansion.
  • Boulder Valley School District Closures Comments: Several residents urged council to advocate for a pause on BVSD plans to close neighborhood schools, citing lack of coordination with the comprehensive plan and housing goals. Speakers argued that declining enrollment stems from high housing costs and affordability, and asked council to request clear answers from the district. Staff said the district holds the final decision and the city has been coordinating with BVSD on future school site uses.
  • Band Shell Seating Redesign and Landmark Demolition Comments: Speakers asked council not to call up the Landmarks Board decision rejecting the Parks Department proposal to demolish the Glenn Huntington Bandshell seating. They argued the historic wooden seats are integral to a city landmark, the redesign with concrete benches and turf lawns is costly and environmentally unsound, and it could invite camping. Speakers requested the Parks Department return with a design that preserves the seats.
  • CU South Open Space Closure Comments: Residents spoke about the planned full closure of CU South open space during flood mitigation construction, which may last three to five years. Speakers requested that the closure be minimized in area and duration, that partial public access be explored, and that a parking lot be provided for access to the remaining open space. Staff responded that full closure is necessary due to construction staging and environmental restoration on the 119 acres the city now owns, and committed to publishing a fuller explanation online.
  • Wildfire Risk and University Hill Density Concerns: A University Hill resident and fire adapted ambassador raised concerns about a proposed 13-bedroom duplex near the wildland urban interface and the cumulative density of student rentals on Grant Place. She asked why the city is not educating residents about high wildfire risk and cited Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan policy on fire adapted communities. Council members later asked staff about the impact of density on evacuation and life safety.
  • Consent Agenda Approval: Council reviewed the consent agenda, with Council Member Shuhart and Council Member Spear voting no on item 4D (FAA grant obligations for the airport) and item 4F (county commissioner seat reorganization), and Council Member Benjamin voting no on item 4F. The remaining items passed unanimously, and the consent agenda was approved.
  • Call-Up of Landmark Alteration for Bandshell and Non-Conforming Use at 969 10th Street: Council voted to call up the landmark alteration certificate for changes at the Glenn Huntington Bandshell, which passed on a show of hands. Council also voted 7-1 to call up a non-conforming use review for an expansion of an existing duplex at 969 10th Street, to take a closer look at whether it meets all applicable criteria.
  • Ordinance 8765: Bird Stova House Landmark Designation: Council held a public hearing on the second reading of Ordinance 8765 to designate 1004 Lincoln Place as an individual landmark known as the Bird Stova House. Staff described the 1920s Craftsman and Tudor Revival home, its association with the Stova family and research in biofeedback, and its location in the potential University Hill historic district. The ordinance was adopted unanimously.
  • Ordinance 8766: Hileman Bedell Stefanic Property Landmark Designation: Council held a public hearing on the second reading of Ordinance 8766 to designate 844-850 12th Street as an individual landmark known as the Hileman Bedell Stefanic Property. Staff described the Southwest Mediterranean style house designed by David Hull Holmes, the first owner's Red Cross service, and the accessory house. The ordinance was adopted unanimously.
  • Ordinance 8770: Repeal of Marijuana Cultivation Energy Offset Requirements: Staff recommended repealing energy offset requirements for marijuana cultivation in BRC chapters 14 and 16, since cultivation now represents a small share of emissions, licensed cultivators have fallen from about 44 to nine, and enforcement consumes significant staff time. The Cannabis Licensing Advisory Board and Environmental Advisory Board supported the change. One speaker opposed the repeal, and the ordinance was adopted unanimously.

entry.title: Boulder: September 10, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session - 2027 Recommended Budget
entry.content:
Most discussed: Budget, Council governance, Wildfire, Parks & recreation, Elections & ballot measures, Water & flooding

  • Opening remarks and 2027 budget overview by City Manager and CFO: City Manager Nuria Rivera-Vandermark introduced the 2027 recommended budget, noting hard trade-offs and reductions after several years of constrained revenue. CFO Christa Morrison presented the total of $552.6 million across all funds, a $135.4 million capital budget, and a 2.3% operating increase, the second slowest since the pandemic. She described sales tax dependence, inflation pressures, and personnel costs making up 41% of operating spending.
  • Budget officer presentation on revenues, assumptions and community engagement: Budget Officer Charlotte Husky outlined budget assumptions including a $6.3 million general fund gap and reductions made in response. Revenue changes include a transportation maintenance fee, a recreational marijuana sales tax increase from 3.5% to 5.5%, and utility fee increases. The Fund Our Future community conversations with over 500 residents informed priorities such as wildfire, facilities maintenance, public safety, and affordable housing.
  • Operating budget changes by goal area: Scott Carpenter, principal budget analyst, highlighted operating changes across the sustainability, equity, and resilience goals. Items included a $4.3 million increase for city facilities maintenance, $11 million in wildfire spending, three new police lieutenant positions, and affordable housing funding for the Alpine Balsam site. Trade-offs included reduced funding for Spruce Pool, elimination of child watch at East Boulder Community Center, and a reduction in the photo enforcement program.
  • Six-year capital improvement program and long-term financial strategy: Budget staff presented the 2027 to 2032 capital improvement program totaling $827.7 million, including utility pipeline repairs, bus priority signal improvements, wildfire prevention projects on open space, and replacement of fire stations 2 and 4. The long-term financial strategy, a comprehensive plan expected in December, and the 2026 November recreation and safety bond were also covered. The community, culture, resilience and safety tax was extended permanently by voters in 2025.
  • Council questions on Alpine Balsam cost history and capital project transparency: Council Member Rob Winer raised concerns about how the Alpine Balsam project's costs and obligations have been communicated and asked how the city can be more transparent on large projects. Deputy City Manager Chris Massey said the project has stayed within council-approved budgets and that a project page and story map covering the 11-year history were published. Staff committed to considering how to tag cross-departmental projects more visibly.
  • Facilities reserves, 2% CRV set-aside and building maintenance bond: Council Member Kaplan asked whether reserves are set aside for future building replacement. Staff explained the 2% capital renewal value set-aside policy and the $4.3 million added for critical facility maintenance enabled by the 3% CCRS tax. Staff said that if the November bond fails, the city would face difficult trade-offs in keeping 15 priority buildings operating.
  • Fund our future priorities, uniform service tiers, and trade-off framework: Council members asked how the new service tier framework (critical, mandated, strategic priority, community enrichment) would guide future budgets and why top community priorities were not more clearly itemized. Staff described the tiering exercise and said it will be tied to work planning. Council Member Benjamin said community priorities such as wildfire, infrastructure, and public safety were spread across the budget and difficult to find.
  • Pools, silver sneakers discounts, and dedicated revenue restrictions: Mayor Pro Tem Tara Winer asked whether Spruce Pool could be funded through the sugar-sweetened beverage tax or whether senior discounts could be income-based. Staff explained that voter-approved uses of those dedicated funds limit reallocation, and that Parks and Recreation is working on how best to serve older adults through a means-tested approach. The high share of restricted revenue citywide was also noted.
  • Internal and external auditor functions: Council Member Winer asked how community members can request an external performance audit and how a project could be audited. Deputy City Attorney Roberto Ramirez referred to a confidential memo on the process. Staff explained the internal auditor works from an annual risk-based plan, that an audit request webpage was recently launched, and that a follow-up discussion on auditing could be scheduled.
  • Wildfire funding, nature-based solutions and grants: Council Members Matt and Rob Winer proposed directing about $2 million in climate initiatives funds and additional OSMP funds toward wildfire mitigation, citing community concern about wildfire risk. Mayor Brockett and other members said they would not support that large a cut in climate funding without more analysis. Staff described nature-based wildfire work, circular economy efforts, and roughly $2.1 million in wildfire grants received.
  • Snow and ice removal and photo enforcement program: Council Member Winer asked whether snow and ice removal would expand to west Boulder streets where seniors are at risk of being stuck. The director of transportation said funds allow for added equipment but not new streets this year, with a packet to come. Winer also asked why the photo enforcement van program was reduced; staff said cost outpaced revenue and officers would prioritize neighborhood complaints.
  • Council budget amendment process and next steps: The deputy city attorney and budget officer explained that council members may propose substantive changes through the hotline by September 28, with an identified offset required for any balanced amendment. The first reading is October 1 and adoption October 15. Council members discussed the timing of any wildfire or other ongoing funding decisions, and the difference between the annual budget and mid-year appropriations.
  • Council closing comments and substantive requests: Council members closed by reiterating concerns on Spruce Pool and the day services center, which are funded with one-time dollars, and asked how to sustain them. Council Member Adams raised concerns about evacuation, recovery and relocation funding, energy rate increases, the water supply under drought scenarios, and reduced outreach funding for community connectors. Mayor Brockett closed the meeting at 8:56 p.m. and reminded members of the September 28 hotline deadline.

entry.title: Boulder: September 3, 2026 Boulder City Council Special Meeting and Regular Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Housing, Public comment, Legal & litigation, Parks & recreation, Transportation, Open space

  • Special Meeting Executive Session: Council convened a special meeting and voted unanimously to enter executive session to receive confidential legal advice regarding authorized uses of city open space. Council returned to public session after the executive session concluded at 5:17 p.m. with no concerns raised on the record.
  • Public Comment on Frasier Meadows Expansion and Panka Place Vacation: Many residents spoke against the Frasier Meadows expansion, a 55-foot, 96-unit senior living project, and the proposed vacation of Panka Place. Concerns included height and setback exemptions, neighborhood transition, traffic, emergency access, flood and wildfire evacuation, and the loss of a public street. Several residents asked council to call up the planning board decision for a public hearing.
  • Public Comment on School Closures and Neighborhood Schools: Residents, including a Flat Irons Elementary second grader, spoke against BVSD's proposed closure of neighborhood schools. Speakers argued the closures affect housing, traffic, climate, and walkable neighborhoods, and asked council to request a one-year delay of BVSD's vote.
  • Public Comment on Student Rentals, Party Houses, and Noise: Residents described party houses and stealth dorm conversions in the Hill and Grant Place areas, citing noise, trash, and loss of affordable long-term rentals. Staff said code compliance tracks noise violations and reaches out to landlords as thresholds approach, and council members asked for follow-up data and possible out-of-the-box solutions.
  • Public Comment on Spruce Pool Funding and Closure: Swimmers and residents testified about the value of Spruce Pool for safety, rehabilitation, overflow aquatics, and history, and opposed proposed funding cuts for 2027 and no funding indicated for 2028. Parks and Recreation staff acknowledged the concern, said the pool is funded for one year, and committed to meeting with supporters.
  • Council Recognition of Mark Wallik and Pollinator Appreciation Month: Council Member Spear read a personal tribute and the joint declaration honoring former council member Mark Wallik's seven years of service. Council Member Shuhart read the declaration for Pollinator Appreciation Month and staff presented the new citywide bee biomonitoring initiative.
  • Consent Agenda and Employee Evaluations: Council approved the consent agenda 8 to 0 with one nay on item 4E, the 2025-26 performance evaluations and salary adjustments for the city manager, city attorney, and municipal judge. Members praised the staff evaluations and raised concerns about the evaluation process and oversight.
  • Call-Up Check-In: Frasier Meadows Site Review and Panka Place: Council discussed the site review amendment for the Frasier and Mountain View United Methodist properties at 350 and 355 Panka Place, including the 55-foot, 96-unit building and private drive with public access easement. Staff addressed flood, energy, and affordable housing fee questions, and a motion to call up the project failed for lack of a second.
  • Call-Up Check-In: Excel Energy Facility Expansion: Council reviewed a concept plan to expand the Xcel Energy service and operations facility at 2655 North 63rd Street. Staff confirmed the project is not related to the Cosmo coal ash remediation work, and no member requested a call-up.
  • Public Hearing: Pedal Cab Agency and Driver Licenses: Council held a public hearing and second reading of Ordinance 8757 creating agency and driver licenses for pedal cabs, including insurance, background checks, traffic compliance, and a ban on selling products while operating. Council approved the ordinance 7 to 0 after staff explained the licensing framework modeled on Denver and Colorado Springs.
  • Matters: State Legislation on Prop 123, TOC Bill, and HOME Act: Staff briefed council on three state laws: Proposition 123 fast-track review for affordable housing, the Transit Oriented Communities bill requiring housing opportunity goals near transit, and the HOME Act for qualifying properties on underutilized land. Council gave direction to pursue removing call-ups for form-based code reviews and affordable projects, and to explore reducing ground floor retail requirements.
  • Restaurant and Small Business Task Force Proposal: Council Members Tina and Matt proposed informal conversations among restaurant owners, workers, and business groups to build relationships and explore mutually beneficial solutions. Council unanimously gave direction to pursue the idea without creating an official task force or staff workload.
  • Council Position on Boulder County Ballot Measure to Expand Commissioners: Council discussed whether to support the Boulder County ballot measure to change the board of county commissioners from three to five members. Members debated whether it is appropriate for the city to weigh in on another governing body's structure, with concerns about districting and representation. Council gave direction 5 to 3 to take a support position.

entry.title: Boulder: August 27, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session - Excel Energy Partnership Update and Wildfire Resilience
entry.content:
Most discussed: Public comment, Wildfire, Council governance, Energy & utilities, Emergency management, Climate & sustainability

  • Excel Energy Partnership Update: Excel Energy presented progress under the 2020 franchise and energy partnership agreement, including 100% emissions-free electricity goals, 85% carbon-free by 2030, and emissions reductions of about 60% achieved by end of 2025. Excel described wildfire mitigation work, including AI panel cameras, enhanced power line safety settings, undergrounding of three feeders, and a transmission rebuild in two phases. Council members pressed on frequent outages, restoration communication, rate impacts, rolling outage risk, and customer service issues.
  • Wildfire Resilience Home Hardening Hub and Mitigation Priorities: Staff presented a council priority project on wildfire resilience, including a draft home hardening implementation hub to connect homeowners to guidance, incentives, and mitigation actions. Staff also presented a project inventory of about 137 projects grouped into 25 programs, 10 tier one priorities, and a draft WOOI risk index dividing the western wildland-urban interface into 12 sections. Council asked about contractor lists, renter participation, mandatory retroactive home hardening, funding models, and measurable 2030 targets.
  • Public Comment and Council Questions Closing: Council members gave short closing comments to Excel and staff, emphasizing reliability, transparency, customer service, and the need for measurable goals. Staff committed to follow-up responses and an October return for further discussion.

entry.title: Boulder: August 20, 2026 Regular City Council Meeting (Boulder)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Development projects, Parking, Transportation, Budget, Economic development, Bikes & pedestrians

  • Agenda amendment and opening open comment: Council moved to remove item 3D (annexation petition for Cherryville and Murley Lane properties) and add item 3J, a resolution supporting the Boulder County early childhood care and education mill levy and a resolution stating the city's positions on 2026 state ballot measures. The motion passed 8-0. Council then opened open comment and the clerk reviewed participation rules.
  • Open comment: hunting amendment, Gaza, Flat Irons wildfire housing, and taxes: Residents spoke on several subjects. Melinda Marquis opposed Initiative 302, the hunting constitutional amendment on the November ballot. Speakers urged divestment from companies linked to Gaza and Israel and a ceasefire resolution. Walt Morgan asked for a pause on high-density student housing permits in the wildland urban interface because of evacuation risk. Rob Smoke raised divestment and AIPAC, and Lynn Seagull objected to tax increases. Staff said a wildfire home-hardening presentation is planned for August 27.
  • Flock license-plate-reader contract pause: Council members asked about the status of the automated license plate reader (Flock) process. Staff said a pause has been put on the request for proposals, but month-to-month camera use with the current provider continues. Staff said a community engagement plan and additional guardrails for civil liberties and privacy would be shared before any contract is finalized.
  • Consent agenda and bond ballot measure discussion: Council discussed consent agenda items, including ordinance 8758 on a proposed bond measure of more than $400 million. Speakers raised concerns about transparency, community trust, and the budget. Staff said a community advisory panel for capital projects is being considered, and that the city has hired an auditor. Council discussed the Alpine Balsam housing funding and confirmed affordable housing fund money is not going to the Western City campus. The consent agenda passed unanimously.
  • Call-up check-in and suspension of rules for public hearings: The council did not call up item 4A, a landmark alteration certificate to relocate an accessory building at 1733 Canyon Boulevard. Council voted unanimously to suspend procedural rules to allow three public hearings during the meeting.
  • Public hearing: North 30th Street property acquisition (Ordinance 8771): Transportation staff requested authority to acquire permanent and temporary easements on about 50 properties for the North 30th Street safety improvements project, through negotiation or eminent domain if needed. The project costs about $9.3 million, with a $7.46 million federal grant and $1.87 million in city funds. Council voted unanimously to adopt Ordinance 8771. No public speakers appeared.
  • Public hearing: South 30th Street property acquisition (Ordinance 8772): Staff requested the same type of property authority for the South 30th Street multimodal improvements project, which connects to Baseline Road and is mostly small temporary easements. The project is about $3.67 million, with a $3 million federal grant and about $670,000 local match. Staff said landscaping on private property would be coordinated with owners and meet zeroscape standards. Council voted unanimously to adopt Ordinance 8772.
  • Public hearing: Sale of KGID-owned parking lot at 2121 Broadway to MALR Boulder LLC: The Downtown Commercial District board considered a purchase agreement to sell the Spruce and Broadway surface lot (59 spaces) to MALR Boulder LLC for a boutique hotel of about 110 rooms, with a proposed price of $5.8 million. The agreement includes 30-year community benefit covenants covering affordable commercial space, public space, arts, local hiring, and energy performance. Staff said a parking study found the lost spaces could be absorbed by nearby garages and that the hotel must still complete full development review. Many residents, churches, and businesses opposed the sale over parking access, while others supported the hotel's economic and vibrancy benefits. The board approved the agreement 7 to 1.
  • Council discussion and water and energy concerns on the hotel: Council members expressed support for the hotel project, while noting the importance of engaging the church and other parking users. Councilmember Taisha raised water supply concerns, noting the 2025 severe-scenario projections were not included, and asked for higher energy and equity standards. Councilmember Rob noted projected revenue from the hotel over 30 years. The motion passed 7 to 1, with one vote against.

entry.title: Boulder: August 13 2026 City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting and Study Session
entry.content:
Most discussed: Council governance, Budget, Development projects, Elections & ballot measures, Boards & appointments, Economic development

  • Special Meeting: Executive Session Motion and Recess: Council convened the special meeting and held a roll call. Council voted unanimously to call an executive session under state statute and charter section 21A2 to receive confidential legal advice regarding potential new litigation. The motion was properly noticed, and the council recessed into executive session.
  • Executive Session Conclusion and Special Meeting Adjournment: The executive session concluded at about 6 PM with participants identified for the record, and no violations of open meetings law were raised. The special meeting was reconvened and closed at 6:01 PM. The study session then began under Council Member Spear.
  • Strategic Planning Check-In for 2027-2030 Citywide Strategic Plan: Staff presented the process for developing the 2027 through 2030 citywide strategic plan, including a staff advisory team, a world of possibilities document with about 41 inputs drawn from over 170 proposals, and a prioritization tool. Council raised concerns about budget transparency, council ownership of the plan, the scoring methodology, and the need to add items such as Title 9 reform and budget process reform. Staff committed to community engagement in November, a November 14 workshop, and a final draft by January.
  • Civic Area East Bookend Development Partnership RFP: Staff presented the civic area east bookend redevelopment, with an optional west bookend, seeking a private development partner to realize community goals for a year-round farmers market, arts and culture, and food uses connected to Boulder Creek Park. The RFP is planned for late summer 2026, with partner selection in early 2027 and concept planning through 2027. Council asked about selection committee membership, park safety and maintenance costs, phasing, the Arapahoe Pathway, and whether any funding has been secured. Council provided feedback that the goals should be stated more explicitly and that affordability and economic synergy should be considered.
  • 2026 State and County Ballot Measures: Staff summarized the Boulder County early childhood care and education mill levy and several state ballot initiatives, including measures on fentanyl penalties, immigration reporting, transportation funding, the graduated income tax, natural gas rights, and conservation sales tax revenue. Council used straw polls to direct staff to draft resolutions opposing the fentanyl and immigration reporting measures and supporting the county child care measure, the graduated income tax, and the education funding measure. Council did not reach consensus on the conservation sales tax measure, and the transportation and natural gas measures were also opposed.

entry.title: Boulder: August 6, 2026 - Boulder City Council Regular Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Public comment, Development projects, Elections & ballot measures, Budget, Parks & recreation, Open space

  • Open Comment Period: Residents spoke during open comment on topics including Palestine and Israel, the Fort Chambers interpretive design, Spruce Pool repairs, permanently affordable housing HOA costs, shelter sanitary conditions, and council investment divestment. Staff responded on open space, Spruce Pool closure through Labor Day, HOA affordability, and the shelter bathroom issue. Council members commented on tribal consultation and investment portfolio governance.
  • Consent Agenda and Call-Up Check-Ins: Council passed the consent agenda items 3A through 3C. Three outside city utility permit requests for properties on Cherryville Road, Frying Pan Road, and Cottonwood Drive were reviewed during call-up check-ins and none were called up.
  • Ballot Measures Staff Presentation: Staff presented five potential November 2026 ballot measures: the recreation and safety bond, the residential vacancy excise tax, the firefighter collective bargaining charter amendment, the debt limit charter amendment, and the downtown development authority. Staff explained financial pressures, the long-term financial strategy, facilities backlog of 15 priority buildings, and DDA mechanics including tax increment financing and governance.
  • Public Hearing on Ballot Measures Public Comment: Dozens of residents spoke on the five ballot measures. Supporters of the DDA cited downtown vacancies and small business needs, while opponents cited diversion of dedicated open space and library funds and lack of citizen input. Many speakers, especially from South Boulder, demanded binding language protecting South Boulder Rec Center amenities, and firefighters and the Boulder Chamber urged referral. Others supported the residential vacancy tax.
  • Ordinance 8761 Firefighter Collective Bargaining Charter Amendment: Council unanimously adopted Ordinance 8761 to refer to the November 3, 2026 ballot a charter amendment guaranteeing full-time fire department employees the right to bargain collectively. The measure was negotiated with IAFF Local 900 leadership and city staff.
  • Ordinance 8758 Recreation and Safety Bond: Council adopted Ordinance 8758 as amended to refer a general obligation bond for recreation, public safety, and capital projects to the November ballot. The amendment changed South Boulder Rec Center language to specify a lap pool, after debate about specificity and community engagement. Projects include South Boulder Rec Center replacement, North Boulder Rec Center renovation, West Senior Center, a public safety building, and fire station renovations.
  • Ordinance 8759 Residential Vacancy Excise Tax: Council voted 7 to 1 to refer Ordinance 8759 to the November ballot, which would impose a vacancy excise tax of 4,000 per unit on homes occupied 183 days or less per year starting January 1, 2028, with CPI adjustment up to 7,000. Council member Spear voted no. Council discussed possible exemptions such as probate.
  • Ordinance 8762 Debt Limit Charter Amendment: Council unanimously approved Ordinance 8762 to refer to the November ballot an amendment to the Boulder home rule charter changing the city's debt limit calculation from assessed value to actual value, bringing the city in line with other Colorado communities and state statute.
  • Ordinance 8763 Downtown Development Authority: Council debated Ordinance 8763 to form a Boulder Downtown Development Authority and refer it to November ballot. Supporters emphasized revitalizing downtown and University Hill, vacancies, and sales tax decline. Opponents raised concerns about diverting dedicated open space and library funds, nonresident corporate voting, lack of library and county engagement, and climate and water risks. A motion to add a post-approval engagement process failed 4-4. The main motion failed 4-4. Council then gave staff direction to scope next steps for continued community engagement, which received six votes.
  • Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Update Conditions and Amendments: Council considered remaining conditions and recommended amendments to the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan update from planning board, the Board of County Commissioners, and county planning commission. Items included removing the history section, municipal airport policy 79, future land use changes in planning area 2, housing diversity policy 82, rural lands definition, near-transit language, and fire-adapted communities policy 89. Council approved all three motion sets unanimously, accepting staff recommendations, and asked for a future resolution on the history section.

entry.title: Boulder: July 30, 2026 - City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting (Tip Offset Ordinance 8754 Second Reading and Public Hearing; Wildfire Resilience on Open Space Ballot Measure Direction)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Labor & wages, Public comment, Economic development, Council governance, Elections & ballot measures, Budget

  • Roll Call, Quorum, and Agenda Amendment: The Mayor called the special meeting to order and the council took roll call, confirming a quorum. The council voted unanimously to amend the agenda to add item 4A, direction on wildfire resilience on open space ballot measure.
  • Consent Agenda Approval: Council considered consent agenda item 2, consisting of items 2A and 2B, and approved them unanimously by roll call vote.
  • Second Reading and Public Hearing on Tip Offset Ordinance 8754: Staff presented proposed Ordinance 8754 amending the minimum wage chapter to set a local tip offset amount for food and beverage workers, outlining four options and community survey results. Restaurant industry data showed slowing sales, jobs, and visits, while most surveyed workers favored no change to the offset.
  • Council Questions on Tip Offset Presentation: Council members asked about whether the sales tax chart was inflation adjusted and questioned how the status quo option was presented as restaurant savings of $62,800, which staff explained as the amount restaurants currently save under the existing $3.32 offset.
  • Public Hearing on Tip Offset Ordinance: Roughly 28 residents, labor organizers, restaurant workers, business representatives, students, and online participants spoke at two-minute limits. Most urged keeping the scheduled minimum wage increases and the current tip offset, citing rising rents and cost of living, while the Boulder Chamber, Colorado Restaurant Association, and Downtown Boulder Partnership asked for a collaborative task force and relief for restaurants.
  • Council Discussion and Decision on Tip Offset: Council members expressed sympathy for both workers and restaurant owners and broad support for a task force including labor, business, landlords, and experts. Several members said they would keep the current minimum wage schedule, and no motion was made to amend the ordinance, so the existing schedule will proceed.
  • Direction on Wildfire Resilience on Open Space Ballot Measure: Staff sought council direction on whether to pursue a charter amendment or code change for wildfire resilience on open space, noting the Open Space Board of Trustees recommended a charter amendment while staff recommended a code change. Council agreed not to pursue a ballot measure this year and to consider an ordinance instead, with an executive session for legal advice before further action.

entry.title: Boulder: July 23, 2026 - Boulder City Council Special Meeting (Airport Funding and BVCP Public Hearings)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Public comment, Budget, Parks & recreation, Council governance, Legal & litigation, Public health

  • Agenda amendments and consent agenda approval: Council voted unanimously to amend the agenda, removing the BVCP adoption from the agenda and adding items for special counsel appointment and holding the July 30 meeting in person. The consent agenda (items 2A through 2F) was then approved unanimously after brief questions about ballot measure language and a special counsel appointment for code of conduct complaints.
  • BVCP public hearing continued to August 6: Council opened the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan adoption public hearing, which staff introduced before council moved to continue it to August 6. The motion passed unanimously and the item was removed from tonight's deliberations.
  • Airport continued operation: staff presentation and financial scenarios: Staff presented financial scenarios for continued airport operations, including options with and without FAA grants and a range of projected deficits. Staff noted that FAA obligations may extend in perpetuity for land-acquisition grants and that a state infrastructure bank loan is the only alternative financing identified. Options for landing fees, hangar development, solar, and other revenue were reviewed, though none were seen as fully closing the gap.
  • Council questions on airport legal options and closure: Council asked outside counsel about the legal and practical implications of FAA obligations, including perpetuity, litigation timelines and costs, and the possibility of closure through litigation, congressional action, or a replacement airport. Counsel described the process as complex, with low probability and costly litigation paths, and staff noted that the 2017 Santa Monica litigation took about 10 years and roughly $10 million.
  • Public hearing testimony on airport future: Dozens of residents, pilots, business representatives, and neighbors testified. Supporters emphasized emergency response, flight training, youth aviation programs, science research, and economic activity, while opponents raised concerns about noise, lead pollution, perpetual FAA obligations, land use, and the need for a public vote. Testimony also addressed landing fees, unleaded fuel, and comparisons to Santa Monica and Longmont.
  • Council deliberation and votes on FAA grant acceptance: Council members discussed fiscal responsibility, budget pressures, noise, climate, and the risk of perpetuity obligations. A motion to require a one-year delay on perpetuity-covenant FAA grants failed 6-3, and a motion to approve continued operation was amended to require council approval of the next FAA grant with perpetuity obligations, which passed 6-3. The amended motion then passed 8-1 after a further vote. Councilmember Wallik announced his resignation at the end of the meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: June 25, 2026 - Boulder City Council Special Meeting (Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan major update deliberation, 2026 ballot measure polling and Fund Our Future engagement results)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Elections & ballot measures, Budget, Taxes & fees, Council governance, Zoning, Housing

  • Consent agenda and roll call: Council called the special meeting to order and took roll call. The consent agenda (items 2A through 2H) was moved, seconded, and approved, with Council Member Spear voting no on item H and Council Member Wallach abstaining.
  • Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan major update: process and staff overview: Staff presented the continued public hearing (deliberations only, no public testimony) on the major update to the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan. The plan must be adopted in identical form by four bodies: City Council, Planning Board, County Planning Commission, and Board of County Commissioners. Staff outlined a four-motion structure and a second-round schedule with County and Planning Board dates in July and a possible August adoption.
  • Conditions of approval from Planning Board and Board of County Commissioners: Planning Board and the Board of County Commissioners proposed binding conditions covering housing diversity (policy 82), the municipal airport (policy 79), tribal consultation terminology (policies 102 and 103), the 50-year planning history section (pages 14 through 17), and land use designations in area two. Council straw polls kept the original housing diversity language, adopted the airport and tribal language changes that were presented, and kept the history section. Council also approved removing the area two neighborhood one designations except for Gunbarrel, which was changed to rural.
  • Recommended amendments from Planning Board, County Planning Commission and County Commissioners: Council reviewed roughly 14 recommended amendments covering plan introduction language, industrial and residential mixing (rejected), 15-minute neighborhoods (rejected), future land use map changes near Valmont and Folsom and East Boulder (rejected), and renewable energy generation language (adopted). Council adopted several edits, including language on the future of housing (small houses on small lots and multi-unit buildings near transit), streets in future land use objectives, and parking and transit stops in park definitions. Council also adopted the County's language on utility services for health and safety issues.
  • Council-proposed amendments: wildfire and development in ignition zones: Council Member Kaplan proposed adding language to policy 89 requiring the city to consider an integrated approach to wildfire risk, including emergency management planning and egress capacity, when evaluating development that increases residential density in mapped wildfire ignition zones. Council supported adding the language as a recommended amendment, with staff noting it might fit better in the topic spread on natural hazard resilience.
  • Motions to approve the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan major update: Council approved four motions unanimously: approving the major update as documented in the June 25, 2026 staff memo, approving the County Commissioner conditions as indicated by straw poll, approving the recommended amendments as indicated by straw poll, and approving the update with council conditions as indicated by straw poll. Staff will document straw poll results in the minutes.
  • 2026 ballot measure polling results: Pollster Adam Probolsky presented results of a likely-voter survey on infrastructure funding. Recreation centers were the top infrastructure priority, and fire stations and wildfire services scored strongly when framed as essential. A $400 million bond polled better than $200 million, and a vacancy tax on second and third homes had majority support. A permanent parks and recreation tax and general fund debt had mixed or plurality support. Staff asked council which measures to advance.
  • Council direction on 2026 ballot measures: Council unanimously agreed to proceed with a tax increase ballot measure for city facilities and operations. Eight council members supported advancing the $400 million recreation and safety bond, and seven supported advancing the vacancy excise tax for further consideration. Council members noted that these are non-binding straw polls, and that ballot language and a public hearing will come later.
  • Fund Our Future engagement results and long-term financial strategy: Micah Intermill of Gov Strategies and Budget Analyst Stacy Polleycove presented results from the Fund Our Future engagement, which reached 599 residents through eight community conversations and an online survey. Wildfire response and prevention was the strongest priority, with maintenance also prioritized. Renters favored affordable housing investments, while homeowners ranked them low, and the sample skewed toward homeowners. The long-term financial strategy and a comprehensive financial plan are due in November 2026.

entry.title: Boulder: June 18, 2026 Regular City Council Meeting
entry.content:

Staff said they are arranging a meeting with partners and will keep council informed.

Council also asked about the Boulder Valley Comp Plan notice requirements and the status of an investment portfolio review. Staff said an internal review is underway and will be shared with council.

Councilmembers condemned racism and antisemitism, citing an ADL lawsuit against Boulder Valley School District and an antisemitic incident. Council discussed the need for policy, transparency, and accountability.

No council member called either item up.
  • Spring Valley Estates annexation and resolution 1381: Council held a public hearing on the annexation of about 43 acres in Spring Valley Estates with RE initial zoning, approved by election. Staff explained the phased process, required water and road infrastructure, and a local improvement district. Council adopted resolution 1381 unanimously and approved an agreement with the Spring Valley Mutual Water Association. Council discussed DOLA grant timing, the 90-day election blackout, and cost allocation concerns raised by residents.
  • Ordinance 8751 on special festival events: Council held a public hearing and adopted ordinance 8751 unanimously. It creates a permit process and standards for special festival events such as Sundance, updates mobile food vehicle rules, and adds sign code provisions for temporary event signage. Staff said the ordinance would take effect in 30 days and be monitored.
  • Ordinance 8752 on festival liquor licenses: Council held a public hearing and adopted ordinance 8752 unanimously. It allows festival liquor licenses and permits authorized by state law and sets a $150 local application fee for administrative review. Council discussed fee-setting and cost recovery.

entry.title: Boulder: June 11, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session - 2026 State Legislative Session Update
entry.content:
Most discussed: Budget, Wildfire, Energy & utilities, Elections & ballot measures, Regional & state relations, Taxes & fees

  • Overview of 2026 State Legislative Session and City Advocacy: Heather Staer, intergovernmental affairs officer, reviewed the outcomes of the 2026 state legislative session, which ran January 14 to May 13 and passed around 450 of 626 bills. The city took positions on 58 bills, and the state budget was the defining force of the session. The governor had vetoed 12 bills with a final action deadline the following day.
  • State Budget Shortfall and Impacts on Boulder: The Joint Budget Committee had to cut about a billion dollars, leaving little room for new programs, and Medicaid costs are a major driver of the deficit. Senate Bill 135 refers a question to voters on the Taber cap for K-12 funding, and Senate Bill 187 created a Medicaid commission. The direct hit to the city is the elimination of the local retail marijuana sales tax share, about $150,000, while indirect impacts include cuts to multimodal transportation funds and affordable housing finance funds.
  • Immigration Bills and Federal Response: The majority party focused on responding to federal actions, particularly immigration, and Democrats struggled to unite behind a single path. Of five immigration bills, two were killed in committee and one was vetoed, while House Bill 1276 passed to address civil liability for sharing immigration status information and authorize detention center inspections. Other bills responded to federal challenges to mail-in voting and federal orders keeping coal plants open.
  • Priority Bills: Homelessness, AI and Utility On-Bill Repayment: House Bill 1202 passed, creating multi-jurisdictional homelessness authorities and requiring a state homelessness strategy. Senate Bill 189 on automated decisionmaking passed and clarifies city responsibilities for AI use. Senate Bill 148, the city's utility on-bill repayment program, failed in appropriations despite years of work and will be re-evaluated over the interim.
  • Housing, Land Use and Transit-Oriented Development Bills: Several housing bills the city supported passed, including Senate Bill 40 on affordable homeownership and House Bill 1065 creating transit and housing investment zones with an affordable housing tax credit. House Bill 1224 strengthened protections for mobile home park residents. The city opposed House Bill 1114 on minimum lot sizes and House Bill 1308 on lot splitting, both of which failed in committee.
  • Data Center Bills and Clean Energy Legislation: Dueling data center bills, House Bill 1030 offering incentives without energy requirements and Senate Bill 102 setting strict requirements, both failed, and sponsors are expected to return next session. Clean energy wins included plug-in solar passing and House Bill 1226 on coal units, while Senate Bill 208 removing wind as a clean energy standard was defeated. Staff noted the bills preserved local control.
  • Public Safety Bills and Firearm Safety: The city opposed three major bills that would have eroded local and state firearm safety laws, and all three were defeated. The city supported House Bill 1144 placing guardrails on 3D printing of firearms. These items reflect the city's advocacy in an election year.
  • RTD Board Modernization (House Bill 1150): The legislature passed House Bill 1150, reducing the RTD board from 15 to nine members with five elected and four governor-appointed, and redrawing districts. The city sought seven elected members, equity language in gubernatorial nominations, and a lower signature threshold, securing only a return to 250 signatures. Requests for more elected seats and equity language were not granted.
  • Looking Ahead: 2026 Election, Leadership Changes and Budget Outlook: The November 2026 election will determine control of the General Assembly, with Democrats likely retaining control but a possible shift between moderate and progressive factions. New legislative leadership and a new governor may change priorities, and the budget may require a special session. Staff expects a budget forecast in mid to late June.
  • November 2026 Ballot Measures Overview: Heather Staer reviewed the ballot measures, including Initiatives 85, 95, 108, 109 and 110 that are officially on the ballot, and the referred measure Senate Bill 135 on retaining revenue above the Taber cap. Initiative 175 on dedicating transportation taxes to roads was expected to be verified soon, and Initiatives 177 and 195 were in circulation. The council may take positions via resolution at a future meeting.
  • Council Discussion of Ballot Measures and Next Steps: Council members raised concerns about Initiatives 95, 108, 109, 110, 85 and 175, noting potential harms to vulnerable communities and state funding, and asked who backs the measures. Council requested staff research and summaries on each measure, including Initiative 175, before deciding whether to take positions by resolution. Staff will bring back additional analysis at a future meeting.
  • Council Questions on Grants, Data Centers and Wildfire-Related Utility Reliability: Council asked about the aggregate fiscal impact of a failed Taber cap increase, the comparative marijuana tax impact on other communities, and data center bill status. Council also asked about collective action on wildfire and power reliability, and staff noted a PUC reauthorization included quality of service plans. Staff said they would look into the grant success rate and monitor state budget forecasts.

entry.title: Boulder: June 4, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting (Joint Public Hearing with Planning Board on Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Major Update)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Zoning, Public comment, Council governance, Regional & state relations, Housing, Equity & civil rights

  • Pride Month Declaration and Proclamation Remarks: Mayor Brockett read a declaration commemorating June 2026 as Pride Month, honoring the Stonewall legacy and Boulder's LGBTQ+ community. Representatives from Rocky Mountain Equality spoke in response and thanked the council. Councilmember Mark gave a point of personal privilege condemning a student group's statement about a June 2025 attack, and the district attorney's statement was also read into the record.
  • Consent Agenda Approval: Council considered consent agenda items 2A through 2F, which covered several routine items. A motion and second were made, and the consent agenda was approved unanimously on a roll call vote.
  • Joint Public Hearing Opening and Staff Presentation on Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Update: Staff introduced the recommended major update to the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan, which was developed over about 20 months with more than 70 engagement opportunities and over a thousand comments. Presenters outlined goals for inclusive process, values-based approach, 104 usable policies, and a simplified 12-designation future land use strategy. Highlights included equity, housing supply, mobility, economic vitality, natural resources, Vision Zero, climate resilience, and city-county governance.
  • Approval Process, Review Roles and Schedule: Christopher Johnson explained that four bodies must approve the identical plan, with the city council and planning board handling all policies and map changes and county bodies reviewing county-related items. Council and planning board will deliberate separately on June 16 and June 25, with a county joint hearing on June 11. Any substantive amendments must be reconciled across all bodies, which could extend the timeline into summer or fall.
  • Council Questions on Land Use Map Changes, Maintenance Funding and Wildfire-Area Density: Council asked for a delta map showing land use changes since the last draft, and staff agreed to prepare one for the June 16 meeting. Council members raised concerns about funding for long-term facility maintenance and affordable housing targets, and staff pointed to updated policies on asset maintenance and funding. Questions about increasing density near the wildland-urban interface led staff to explain that rezoning and public review would be needed before any such increase.
  • Questions on Industrial Land Use, Residential Uses and Displacement Concerns: Council members asked whether residential uses are prohibited in industrial designations and whether existing industrial businesses would be protected from displacement. Staff explained that zoning still governs allowed uses, that site review is more discretionary than use review, and that existing industrial tenants have limited protections under the plan. Staff noted that the plan aims to create housing elsewhere to reduce pressure on industrial land.
  • Questions on Affordable Housing Goal, Implementation and Indigenous Partnership: Council asked why the plan keeps a 15 percent affordable housing goal, and staff said the goal is aspirational and was set to be ambitious. Members asked how the plan will move from policy to action, and staff pointed to the upcoming citywide strategic plan and council priority setting. A council member raised the need for stronger commitments to indigenous communities, including land back.
  • Questions on Planning Areas, Subcommunity Planning, Groundwater and Process for Proposed Amendments: Council and planning board members questioned how amendments should be submitted, with staff advising that suggestions go to staff rather than through a public hotline to avoid serial meetings. Members asked about the future of subcommunity and area planning guidance, the IGA for the Area 3 planning reserve, and groundwater protection, which the state regulates. Staff confirmed the IGA runs through 2042 and will be revisited.
  • Public Hearing Procedures and Public Testimony: Alicia read the public participation guidelines, and 17 speakers signed up with two-minute limits. Speakers raised concerns about land use designations changing residential and industrial zones, housing types and density, middle-income housing, notification of property owners, the survey's design, water supply and wildfire risk, and the process used to develop the plan. Some speakers supported the plan and its inclusive process and called for restoring residential uses in industrial designations.
  • Clarifying Questions on Notification, Survey Methods and Outreach Demographics: Staff explained that property owners were notified through a utility billing insert because mailing 55,000 letters was not feasible, and the city attorney confirmed legal notice requirements were met. Staff said the survey was developed with a national consultant, and clarified that outreach was open to all residents without a specific 25 percent focus on college students. Council members also asked about how outreach reached renters and homeowners.
  • Planning Board Continuance Motion: The planning board chair asked for a motion to continue the item to June 16, 2026, for planning board deliberation and action. The motion was made and seconded, and it passed seven to zero. No additional public comment will be taken at that meeting, though emails will be read.
  • Council Continuance Motion and Adjournment: Council moved to continue the item to June 25, 2026, for council deliberation and action on the plan, with no additional public comment at that meeting. The motion was seconded and passed unanimously. The mayor thanked staff and planning board members and adjourned the meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: May 28, 2026 Boulder City Council Special Meeting and Study Session
entry.content:
Most discussed: Economic development, Council governance, Taxes & fees, Budget, Transportation, Legal & litigation

  • Consent Agenda: Council Endorsement of Matt Benjamin's CML Executive Board Nomination: Council voted to add item 2A to the consent agenda confirming endorsement of Councilmember Matt Benjamin's nomination to the Colorado Municipal League Executive Board. Benjamin explained CML's role lobbying state legislation and Boulder's two appointed seats. Benjamin recused himself, and the consent agenda passed 8 to 0.
  • Public Hearing: Ordinance 8749 Eminent Domain for Arapahoe Avenue Safety Project: Staff presented the Arapahoe Avenue safety improvement project, a $12 million effort with $9.6 million in federal funding and $2.4 million in city funds. Acquiring about 700 square feet from each of 14 properties may require eminent domain authority to keep the schedule and meet the 2030 federal spending deadline, though staff does not expect to use it. One resident spoke against the ordinance during public comment. Council unanimously adopted Ordinance 8749.
  • Matters: Council Direction on Continued Use of Airport Land: Staff asked whether the question of continuing airport operations indefinitely should return as a consent item or a public hearing. Council members favored a public hearing for community input, and a majority voted for that path. Council also directed staff, by a vote of five, to bring back two options and legal research on long-term land encumbrance and FAA grant implications.
  • Study Session: Downtown Development Authority (DDA) Formation Analysis: Staff presented the draft DDA plan of development, a 30-year reinvestment framework covering downtown, University Hill, and connecting corridors. Financing would rely on a 3.67 mill levy replacing existing GID levies, tax increment financing, and parking asset integration. Staff requested direction on feedback to the plan, the financial structure, and drafting ballot measures for November 2026. Council members raised concerns about general fund impacts, parking governance, equity for the Hill, and measuring outcomes, and generally supported moving forward.

entry.title: Boulder: May 21, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Meeting (Regular Meeting)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Council governance, Elections & ballot measures, Affordable housing, Budget, Housing, Transportation

  • Open Comment: San Lazaro Mobile Home Park Purchase: Multiple San Lazaro residents and a steering committee spoke in Spanish and English through interpretation, describing displacement fears, rising lot rents under private equity ownership, and a $42.5 million purchase offer. Speakers asked the city to help residents buy the park and to raise the issue with Boulder County. Council members and staff responded that the city supports the effort, is coordinating with the county, and is splitting the cost of a new appraisal. Staff said financial support options are being explored.
  • Open Comment: Boulder Municipal Airport and FAA Local Control: Several residents urged council to place a ballot measure before voters on keeping local control of the municipal airport rather than accepting FAA grants that impose long-term obligations. Speakers raised noise, leaded fuel, and enforcement concerns, and cited airports in Santa Monica and Torrance as examples of local control. A speaker also said council's recent study session on the airport relied on incomplete information and asked for a do-over. Staff responded that funding decisions depend on future land use and that CDOT funding limits had been misstated, with the topic to return to council.
  • Open Comment: Golden West Utilities and Lease Changes: Golden West Manor residents, many of them seniors on fixed incomes, said cable, TV, and telephone services will no longer be included in their leases starting September 1, and that parking now costs $50 per month. They also raised elevator reliability problems in the 14-story building. Staff said the Comcast contract is ending, free Wi-Fi will continue with a rent reduction of about $40 to $45, and Boulder Housing Partners will provide support for transitioning residents.
  • Open Comment: Other Public Comments on Wages, Housing, and Civic Issues: Speakers addressed a range of topics including opposition to the tipped minimum wage freeze and support for a vacancy tax, a request for a streamlined city process for tree-protection and lot reviews, and a proposal for Colorado independence. Other speakers raised concerns about federal actions, international conflicts, and the rights of residents. Council members and staff thanked speakers and responded briefly.
  • Consent Agenda Items 3A and 3B: Council approved the consent agenda with a motion and second. Councilmember Wallach voted no on item 3B, an ordinance amending Title 7 height limitations, citing imprecise drafting. Items 3A and 3B passed unanimously otherwise.
  • Call-Up Check-Ins: 777 Broadway Site Review and 990 Arapahoe Landmark: No council members called up the 777 Broadway site review for redevelopment with 63 residential units, or the Landmarks Board decision not to designate 990 Arapahoe Avenue as an individual landmark. Mayor Pro Tem Weiner used the landmark item to suggest reviewing the landmarking process at next year's retreat, citing conflicts with affordable housing and displacement.
  • Public Hearing: First Adjustment to Base Budget (ATB1) and Ordinance 8750: Staff presented ATB1, an $18.6 million budget adjustment including $13.1 million from fund balance, $5.3 million in mid-year grants, and $129,000 in additional revenue. Most fund balance draws are restricted to specific purposes such as radio replacement for public safety, affordable housing projects, and wildfire programs. The public hearing included comments on the budget and a discussion of communications staffing. Council unanimously adopted Ordinance 8750.
  • Matters: Study Session Procedures, Straw Polls, and Reconsideration: City Attorney Teresa Taylor Tate explained that official action occurs only at regular or special meetings, while study sessions provide non-binding direction to staff. Council discussed how straw polls function, what counts as a material change warranting reconsideration, and how consent items and calls-up work. Council agreed to add non-binding language for straw polls and to clarify that study sessions may include information-only items, with staff to provide a summary of look-ahead agenda items.

entry.title: Boulder: May 14, 2026 Boulder City Council Study Session: Financial Forecast and 2026 Ballot Measures
entry.content:
Most discussed: Budget, Taxes & fees, Housing, Elections & ballot measures, Council governance, Economic development

  • Economic Conditions and Financial Forecast Presentation: CU Boulder's Business Research Division presented economic conditions affecting Boulder sales and use tax, noting modest GDP growth, stalled national employment, Colorado job losses, and rising inflation driven by energy prices. Staff explained that sales and use tax and property tax revenues are flattening and forecasts were lowered for 2026 and 2027. Council members asked about recession risk, federal policy impacts, and the Federal Reserve's stance. The forecast uses a medium economic scenario with statistical bounds.
  • 2026 and 2027 Budget Shortfalls and Department Reductions: Staff reported that 2025 required a hiring freeze and 5% operating savings to close an 8 to 10 million shortfall, and 2026 required a 7.8% general fund reduction. A $6.5 million general fund shortfall for 2027 prompts requested 4% reductions across departments. The care program was restructured into a cross-functional behavioral health team. Council asked for more transparency on how reductions affect services and the public.
  • Sales and Property Tax Revenue Forecasts: Staff presented sales and use tax actuals and forecasts showing retail sales tax flattening at around 1% annual growth and a forecasted decline in 2026. Property tax projections were revised down by about 7 million due to state legislation and lack of growth, with reassessment growth at only 0.2%. Council asked about the sales to property tax ratio and the impact of Sundance revenue, which will be cautiously incorporated in year one.
  • 2027 Budget Calendar and Process: Staff outlined the 2027 budget timeline: department submissions in mid-June, executive budget team decisions in July, city manager's recommended budget on August 28, a study session on September 10, and first and second readings on October 1 and 15. Council discussed how to provide input and the desire for a two-year budget cycle. Council also asked for budget-versus-actual data at the project level.
  • Long-Term Financial Strategy and Ballot Measure Framework: Staff described the long-term financial strategy, including a comprehensive financial plan due in late 2026, and explained that about 68% of city revenue is already committed to specific purposes. General fund expenses have grown faster than revenue. Staff noted that polling works best with three to four items and that ballot measures should be sequenced with other measures. Council discussed the need to communicate trade-offs clearly to the public.
  • Facilities Investment Needs and Funding Scenarios: Staff reported that 15 priority city buildings, including recreation centers and the public safety building, need about 20 million over five to six years for critical maintenance and roughly 400 million in unfunded priority needs. Five funding scenarios were presented, mixing existing CCRS tax authority, a parks and public improvement mill levy, general obligation debt, and a charter change to the 3% debt limit. Staff recommended scenarios C and E, providing up to 200 million. Council discussed impacts on residents and businesses and the need for polling on specific projects and thresholds.
  • Council Direction on Ballot Measure Polling: Council gave direction to poll on the parks and public improvement mill levy expansion, a 200 million general obligation debt authorization with associated mill levy, and a charter change to the debt limit. Council members expressed mixed views on including the 400 million option, the general fund debt authorization, and the flexibility of language. Staff will bring polling results in late June and return with ballot ordinances in summer.
  • Residential Vacancy Excise Tax Discussion: Staff sought direction on whether to pursue a residential vacancy excise tax, a second homes tax applied to properties vacant at least 183 days. Council members discussed tiered structures based on square footage, higher maximum amounts, whether to use an ordinance rather than a ballot initiative for flexibility, and legal research on the approach. Council members supported further analysis and polling, with some expressing concerns about housing impacts.
  • Charter Amendments: Boards and Commissions and Open Space Wildfire Mitigation: The charter committee recommended revisiting a boards and commissions amendment from 2024, which failed, and adding wildfire mitigation as an explicit purpose of open space under charter section 176. Council discussed removing removal provisions, adding flood mitigation, and the timing of these changes. Council decided not to move boards and commissions forward this year but directed staff to continue research on the wildfire open space amendment.
  • Community Petitions and State and Regional Ballot Measures: Staff noted one community-sponsored petition on commercial and residential vacancy taxes and provided information on potential state of Colorado ballot measures with tax impacts. Boulder County and Boulder Valley School District ballot measures are yet to be determined. A legislative update is planned for June. A council member requested a future meeting to take positions on several potential ballot measures.

entry.title: Boulder: May 7, 2026 Boulder City Council Regular Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Labor & wages, Zoning, Economic development, Historic preservation, Regional & state relations, Public comment

  • Call to order, roll call, and agenda amendment: Council convened the regular meeting and took a roll call with all members present. Council voted unanimously to remove item 4E from the consent agenda, which means the June 11 study session will proceed as usual.
  • Open comment on tipped minimum wage: Multiple residents urged council not to cut the tipped minimum wage, citing the living wage cost in Boulder and the hardship on service workers. Speakers argued that wage cuts would hurt local consumers and the economy and asked council to focus instead on corporate landlords and vacant commercial space.
  • Open comment on residential vacancy tax and housing: Several speakers urged council to place a residential vacancy tax on the ballot and raise the proposed amount from $2,000 to $5,000 per vacant unit. Speakers argued that vacant homes worsen the housing shortage and that a larger tax would be more effective. Speakers also raised concerns about commercial vacancy and tax base erosion.
  • Open comment on Boulder Municipal Airport and FAA grants: Speakers asked council never to accept FAA grants that would commit the city to maintaining the airport in perpetuity. A speaker also criticized an April 23 study session decision to dedicate 175 acres of city land to the FAA and aviation industry, saying the decision relied on unverified information and excluded public input.
  • Open comment on South Boulder Rec Center and other topics: A youth speaker urged council to keep the pool at the South Boulder Recreation Center open, citing the 15-minute city goal. Other speakers raised bike registration, the Charge Bug energy app, an Israel-Gaza divestment request, and concerns about building permit red tape.
  • Staff response and council comments on open comment: Staff said tipped credit changes would come later in the year and that the proposals under consideration would not reduce the tipped minimum wage. Staff committed to follow-up on the lot split question, a health-related concern, and the airport. Council members offered brief comments, including Councilmember Tasha's remarks on a planned July public hearing on tip credit.
  • Consent agenda approval: Council moved and approved the consent agenda, which included items 4A through 4D and 4F through 4L, after clarifying that the beverage licensing rules amendment would be discussed at second reading. The vote was unanimous.
  • National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons declaration: Council Member Adams presented a declaration recognizing May 5 or 6, 2026 as the National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons, signed by Mayor Brockett. Speakers from community organizations urged real action beyond proclamations, including policing training, reparations, and caution about Flock camera surveillance harms to Indigenous communities.
