  • Call-up check-ins for landmark and site review items: Council reviewed several call-up items, including landmark alteration applications for 409 Mountain View Road and the Chestnut and Arapahoe houses, a height modification at 1039 Mapleton Avenue, and a utility permit at 1420 Cherryvale Road. Council discussed a concept plan for 60 units of permanently affordable senior housing at Presbyterian Manor and decided not to call any items up.
  • Public hearing: Landmark designation of 745 University Avenue: Council held the second reading and public hearing to designate 745 University Avenue as the Polls and Registration House, an individual landmark. The house was a municipal polling place for two decades and was tied to Boulder's early proportional voting history. Council unanimously adopted Ordinance 8741.
  • Public hearing: Omnibus land use code amendment (Ordinance 8745): Staff presented an omnibus ordinance to fix errors, clarify code, and amend height, use, and site review standards. Changes include removing office floor area limits, allowing height modifications up to 55 feet for certain community uses on three-story buildings, and clarifying parking in converted garages. Council added an amendment removing outdoor patio size limits for breweries and tap rooms, and the ordinance passed five to one.
  • Adjournment: Council closed the meeting at 9:42 p.m. after completing the agenda.

entry.title: Boulder: April 23, 2026 Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Most discussed: Council governance, Energy & utilities, Budget, Wildfire, Development projects, Emergency management

  • Boulder Municipal Airport Future: Indefinite Operation vs. Closure Opportunity: Staff presented an update on the airport's future, including the dismissed FAA lawsuit, the community conversation results, and financial projections showing scenario two would require about $600,000 per year in local subsidy. Council discussed grant assurances in perpetuity, noise and leaded fuel limits, and redevelopment potential of the land. Council members debated the financial and legal implications and a straw poll favored scenario one, continuing airport operations indefinitely. Staff was directed to bring back a formal action to memorialize the direction.
  • Power Resilience and Public Safety Power Shutoffs: Staff presented on increasing public safety power shutoffs and outages driven by wildfire mitigation and aging infrastructure. The presentation covered Excel Energy's hardening work, reliability metrics, and risk zones, along with a phased community engagement plan including a summer workshop and a fall community council forum. Council expressed support for the approach and asked about accountability, timelines, relocation considerations, and cross-departmental trade-offs. Council confirmed alignment with the proposed approach.

entry.title: Boulder: April 16, 2026 Regular City Council Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Development projects, Economic development, Regional & state relations, Budget, Council governance, Taxes & fees

  • Open Comment Period: Residents spoke during open comment on a range of issues including the transportation maintenance fee exemption for religious buildings, zoning and landmarking reviews, the Boulder Municipal Airport, South Boulder Rec Center funding, bear trash ordinance evaluation, tipped minimum wage, and Flock AI surveillance. Speakers were limited to two or three minutes and staff and council responded briefly to several comments. Council members asked residents to direct criticism at policies rather than individuals or staff.
  • Consent Agenda: Council approved the consent agenda items 3A through 3I unanimously. Questions covered the Spring Valley Estates annexation water lines and resident cost sharing, and Ordinance 8745 on land use code changes, where staff kept the original three-story recommendation rather than the planning board's alteration. Council also discussed a brewery square footage issue to be researched.
  • Metropolitan Districts Ordinance 8748 and Model Service Plan: Staff presented the regulatory framework for metropolitan districts, which limits formation to commercial districts with at least 90 percent non-residential use, sets a 50 mill debt cap and 65 mill aggregate cap, and imposes a 40-year debt discharge rule and a three-mill regional improvements levy. Council questioned the mill levy impacts, voter eligibility, and compounding interest. Council then adopted Ordinance 8748 unanimously, and the model service plan resolution was deferred so staff can add a compounding interest option.
  • Legislative Update and State Advocacy: Intergovernmental affairs staff reviewed the state legislative session, including House Bill 1202 on homelessness, Senate Bill 148 on on-bill energy repayment, AI policy, budget cuts, and the Home Act. Council discussed Senate Bill 150 on RTD reform and House Bill 1308 on lot splitting, and agreed to take an oppose-unless-amended position on 1308 that would move to monitor if three requested amendments are adopted. Council also received a note on a staff award.

entry.title: Boulder: April 9, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Most discussed: Budget, Parks & recreation, Fire & EMS, Taxes & fees, Elections & ballot measures, Arts, culture & libraries

  • Boulder Arts Blueprint update: Staff presented the Boulder Arts Blueprint, a 10-year citywide arts and culture roadmap aligned with the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan and CERG goals. It is organized around seven goals and funded largely through the Arts, Culture and Heritage Tax and the 1% for Art policy. Council asked about staffing capacity, grant funding increases to $2 million, neighborhood reach, the back-of-house services cohort, the 2A tax dependency, Sundance Festival opportunities, and the lack of baseline data and KPIs. Several members supported the direction but asked for measurable metrics, reporting, and attention to artist affordability and prioritization.
  • Facilities investment strategy and recreation center scenarios: Staff presented the facilities investment strategy for roughly 75 city buildings, averaging about 50 years old, with 15 priority buildings including the South Boulder, North Boulder and East Boulder recreation centers. Minimum urgent repairs total about $20 million, while larger modernization projects total roughly $500 million, of which about $400 million is unfunded. Staff recommended prioritizing minimum infrastructure investment with current funds and developing investment scenarios for priority buildings, to return in May alongside possible tax ballot measures. Council questions covered sustainability versus cost, renovation versus new build, fire station consolidation, property disposal, and the unfunded liability definition. Council generally agreed with both recommendations while requesting more financial data and a clearer whole-picture view.

entry.title: Boulder: April 2, 2026 Regular City Council Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Labor & wages, Economic development, Budget, Housing, Parks & recreation, Transportation

  • Open Comment on South Boulder Rec Center and Pool: Many residents, youth, and athletes spoke in favor of preserving the South Boulder Recreation Center and its pool, citing walkability, health, and community value. Speakers criticized the data and options staff presented and urged the city to fund a rebuild or retain core amenities. Several speakers said the center serves as a safe after-school and senior gathering place.
  • Open Comment on Tipped Wage Credit: Several speakers, including tipped workers, a labor organizer, and a health clinic specialist, urged council to oppose any increase to the tip credit, arguing it would cut take-home pay and worsen affordability. Restaurant owners and the Barha representative were not heard in this segment, though one speaker noted small business struggles. Speakers emphasized inflation, wage theft, and inconsistent tips.
  • Open Comment on Other Issues (Airport, Bears, Open Space, Israel and Flock): Speakers addressed unleaded aviation fuel at the airport, bear conflict and electric fencing ordinance updates, and the proposed open space tax ballot measure. One speaker criticized Flock Safety surveillance contracts and called for divestment. Staff responded that the fencing ordinance proposal is under consideration for future council action.
  • Arts Week Declaration: Council presented a proclamation declaring April 3 to 12, 2026 as Boulder Arts Week and recognized Dr. Nicholas Felder as the Bright Futures Award recipient. Felder accepted on behalf of the arts community and spoke to the Boulder Arts Blueprint. Staff noted Boulder's creative sector strength and economic impact.
  • Consent Agenda: Council approved consent agenda items 4A through 4Q, including a 10-year water lease with the Town of Erie and a water supply framework resolution for area 3. Council member Adams voted no on the area 3 service expansion item. Council discussed the Erie lease, which staff said would not jeopardize local water supply during drought watch.
  • Call-Up Items and Site Review at College Avenue: Council reviewed call-up items including a Boulder Jewish Commons synagogue amendment, a water tap request in area 3, and a student housing site review at 1128 29th Street and 2895 East College Avenue. A motion to refer the College Avenue project to the Design Advisory Board was withdrawn after staff said the board had already reviewed and approved the design. Landmark alteration for an accessory building in Mapleton Hill was also listed.
  • Short-Term Festival Lodging Rental Ordinance (Second Reading): Council held a public hearing and adopted Ordinance 8743, expanding festival lodging rental licenses to tenants with owner consent and to vacant units in properties with long-term rental licenses. Staff said applications open the next day and licenses issue May 4 for Sundance. Council discussed revenue splits, renter protections, and a possible vacant-only option that was not adopted, and the vote was 8 to 0.
  • Tip Offset Options and Timeline: Staff presented the tip credit authority options after council's retreat priority and reviewed economic, labor, and equity considerations, including restaurant sales tax and employment trends. Options included status quo, moderate increases, a higher offset, and maximized offset, with council narrowing to status quo, Option 2A, Option 2B, and a Benjamin proposal to pause the tipped wage through 2029. Council directed staff to return with more data and considered a later public hearing aligned with student availability, with CAC to help schedule.

entry.title: Boulder: March 26, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Study Session with Planning Board (Joint Session: BVSD Enrollment Update and Draft Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Review)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Zoning, Housing, Council governance, Regional & state relations, Public comment, Transportation

  • Boulder Valley School District Declining Enrollment Update: BVSD leaders presented on sustained enrollment decline of over 3,600 students since 2017, with a projected further loss of about 1,700 students. They explained that underused buildings divert funds from classrooms and that small schools lose specials, counselors, and collaboration time. The district outlined a community engagement timeline running through fall 2026 with a final plan in October. Council asked about long-term timing, the city's role in any surplus building reuse, and how the community can participate.
  • Draft Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan Overview: Staff presented the draft comprehensive plan update, which reorganizes the document into six chapters and reduces policies from 210 to 102. The draft introduces a simplified future land use map with four classes and twelve designations, a new implementation chapter, and an equity-centered framework. Capacity modeling shows roughly a 35 percent increase in housing opportunities and more balanced housing types. Staff said public comment closes April 6 and a joint four-body meeting is set for April 13, with adoption hearings in June.
  • Council and Planning Board Clarifying Questions on the Draft Plan: Council and planning board members asked whether the plan should be more operational, how many new housing units would come from student populations, and how the land use map relates to existing zoning. Members also raised concerns about transportation language, the airport policy, and how implementation will be measured and funded. Staff explained that zoning rights remain in place until property owners request changes and that department and strategic plans will carry operational detail.
  • Consensus Feedback on Draft Plan Alignment and Strengths: Council and planning board members generally agreed the draft reflects community feedback and praised the simplified land use designations, expanded housing types, and the 15-minute neighborhood concept. Members highlighted the equity-focused first policy, the community assembly's direct influence, and new policies on social infrastructure and the night economy. Several members noted that zoning changes will be needed to realize the new neighborhood designations.
  • Recommended Revisions to Draft Plan Language and Mapping: Members proposed refinements including clearer transportation outcomes and safety language, a definition or alternative to neighborhood character, more neighborhood 2 designations along transit corridors and near downtown and the university, stronger wildfire and fuel management language, and clearer tribal and land-back acknowledgments. Some asked for a policy on built environment design and for limits on converting multiple units into single units. The group did not reach consensus on a straw poll to expand neighborhood 2 designations, with council split and planning board favoring analysis.
  • Next Steps and Milestones for Plan Adoption: Staff asked that comments be sent to the project email by April 6, with a four-body meeting on April 13 to resolve major issues. The recommended plan is scheduled for release on May 18, followed by a joint public hearing on June 4. Staff confirmed the plan takes effect immediately upon final approval by all four bodies.

entry.title: Boulder: March 12, 2026 City Council Study Session
entry.content:
Most discussed: Elections & ballot measures, Development projects, Taxes & fees, Budget, Economic development, Council governance

  • Boulder Strong Day of Remembrance Declaration: Councilmember Wallach presented a declaration designating March 22 as the Boulder Day of Remembrance to honor the 10 people killed in the March 22, 2021 King Soopers mass shooting. The council read the victims' names and announced a remembrance ceremony at the Boulder Museum on March 22 from 3:30 to 4:30 p.m. The declaration was signed by Mayor Aaron Brockett.
  • Downtown Development Authority Formation and Initial Recommendations: Staff presented the proposed Downtown Development Authority, a tax increment financing tool to fund long-term reinvestment in downtown and the Hill, with a study area still under refinement and no final boundaries. Staff recommended exploring a standalone DDA with a 1-2 year transition, a funding model combining a mill levy, property and sales tax increment, and possibly parking assets, with fiscal safeguards. Council asked about voting thresholds, the base year, parking and GID asset transfers, staff costs, liability, and oversight, and generally supported continued refinement toward a November ballot decision.
  • 2026 Ballot Measures and Long-Term Financial Strategy: Finance staff presented the long-term financial strategy, noting that 68% of city revenues are dedicated and that property tax growth has slowed sharply. Staff previewed transformational, mid-range, and structural tax ballot options, including a sales tax on services, a sales-to-property tax swap, a general purpose mill levy, a public realm mill levy, a residential vacancy excise tax, a general fund debt authorization, a mill levy cap increase, and consolidation of dedicated sales taxes. Through straw polls, council narrowed the options to the public realm mill levy, residential vacancy excise tax, general fund debt authorization, and consolidation of dedicated sales taxes, with staff returning in April and May.

entry.title: Boulder: March 5, 2026 - Boulder City Council Regular Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Boards & appointments, Affordable housing, Budget, Council governance, Parks & recreation, Housing

  • Open Comment: Flock Safety Cameras: Multiple residents urged council to cancel or not renew the Flock Safety license-plate-reader contract, citing immigration enforcement concerns, data-sharing risks, security vulnerabilities, and Flock's alleged misconduct. Speakers asked for public votes and data-retention policies, and some pointed to Denver, Longmont, and state legislation as examples. Council members said they were uncomfortable with the vulnerabilities and that staff is developing both near-term contract decisions and a broader policy. Staff noted that policy on surveillance and data sharing falls within council's purview.
  • Open Comment: South Boulder Recreation Center: Many speakers, including seniors, swimmers, parents, and a 10-year-old student, urged council to keep the South Boulder Rec Center open with its pool, gym, and basketball court. Speakers cited crowded pools, the loss of other city pools, walkability, and the 15-minute neighborhood goal. Staff said a study session on facilities funding is scheduled for April 9 that will cover rec centers.
  • Consent Agenda and Item 3E Area Three Guidance: Council pulled item 3E, the Area Three planning reserve resolution, for separate discussion. Council members agreed to revise the language so Area Three housing is not limited to middle-income ownership and can include other housing types such as senior or service-supported housing. Council gave a unanimous straw poll direction to staff, and the remaining consent agenda items were approved unanimously.
  • Call-Up Check-In: 3550 and 3850 Frontier Avenue Redevelopment: Council reviewed a concept plan for a mixed-use redevelopment with a 2,500-capacity events venue, a hotel, about 500 apartments, and commercial space, requiring rezoning and height modifications. Council members said they did not need to call up the project and were open to legislative action if needed to allow it. Staff noted that a tailored zone district may be needed and that council would review specific issues such as inclusionary housing at site review.
  • 2026 Board and Commission Appointments: Council held a public hearing on 2026 board and commission appointments, with two speakers offering general comments. The city clerk explained the nomination and voting process, and council nominated and voted on candidates for each open seat, including the Boulder Urban Renewal Authority. Council unanimously approved the 2026 appointments, with the Urban Renewal Authority appointments taking effect immediately.
  • Affordable Housing Review: Staff presented an overview of Boulder's affordable housing program, including the gap between incomes and home prices, the rental and ownership market, supply and demand programs, and partnerships with Boulder Housing Partners. Staff said the city has produced affordable units at about 37 percent of new development, outperforming its 25 percent inclusionary requirement, and that most local funding comes from local sources. Council asked about middle-income ownership, cash-in-lieu payments, the 15 percent housing goal, unused down-payment funds, and land banking, and staff said next steps include zoning reforms, expanded down-payment assistance, and continued innovation.

entry.title: Boulder: February 19, 2026 Regular City Council Meeting (Boulder City Council)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Development projects, Parks & recreation, Zoning, Public comment, Housing, Economic development

  • Roll Call and Open Comment Procedures: Council convened the regular meeting with roll call confirming a quorum. The clerk reviewed public participation guidelines and rules of decorum for open comment.
  • Open Comment on South Boulder Rec Center Pool: Many residents, students, and Fairview swim team members urged council to keep the South Boulder Rec Center pool and gym, citing proximity for families, seniors, and youth. Speakers questioned the 2025 engineering report and parks department priorities. Staff said no decisions have been made and that more discussions on rec centers are planned for spring study sessions.
  • Open Comment on Other Community Issues: Speakers raised concerns including Middle East policy, dog off-leash trail safety and the Voice and Sight tag program, ambulance sedation allegations against a former provider, property taxes, and climate resilience and microgrids. Council members thanked speakers and staff committed to follow-up on several items.
  • Consent Agenda: Council approved consent agenda items 3A and 3B by unanimous roll call vote.
  • Hogan-Pancost Property Annexation and Land Use Change: Council held a public hearing on annexing about 24 acres at 5399 Kowani Drive and 5697 South Boulder Road, including part of 55th Street, with public zoning and RL-2 for right-of-way. Parks and Recreation proposed flood mitigation and parks use west of 55th, with open space east of 55th. Council adopted Resolution 1370, Ordinance 8734, and the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan land use map change unanimously. Public comment included a botanic garden proposal.
  • Pearl Street Storage Site Concept Review: Council gave feedback on a concept review for redeveloping the Boulder Storage site at 4880 and 4898 Pearl Street with about 281 apartments and a new storage building in a General Industrial zone. Key issues were consistency with the BVCP, the East Boulder subcommunity plan, and the six-percent contiguity rule for residential use. Council members generally wanted to preserve industrial character and asked the applicant to rethink the design and mix of uses. No formal action was taken.

entry.title: Boulder: February 12, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Housing, Development projects, Council governance, Crime & justice, Affordable housing, Public comment

  • Area 3 Planning Reserve Community Needs Assessment (Service Area Expansion Step Two): Staff presented the step two community needs assessment for the Area 3 Planning Reserve, identifying six needs including housing, fire storage, aging-in-place facilities, parkland, agriculture, and renewable energy. Council asked detailed questions about middle-income housing gaps, parkland standards, water, infrastructure costs, and staff capacity. Public speakers largely urged moving forward, while some opposed due to water, traffic, and habitat concerns. Council voted 7-2 to find the identified needs of sufficient priority to warrant further consideration of a service area expansion plan, and gave staff direction to bring back a guiding resolution on consent.
  • Consent Agenda and Agenda Amendment: Council unanimously amended the agenda to remove item 6A and then unanimously approved the consent agenda items 2A and 2B.
  • Community Change Requests Reconsideration Following County Commissioners Action: Staff reviewed five community change requests the Boulder County commissioners wanted reconsidered, including three land use requests near Gunbarrel and two comprehensive plan policies on area 2 annexation. Staff recommended against reconsideration, and council expressed no interest in reconsidering any of them.
  • Municipal Court Update: Presiding Judge Jeff Khan and Court Administrator Devon Kiss Kelly reviewed 2025 case filings, which included rising traffic and photo enforcement, a jump in criminal cases, and increased quality-of-life citations near CU. They highlighted the community court, mental health counseling, parking appeals, and a new data dashboard. They also flagged Colorado Supreme Court's Camp decision and pending public defender legislation as legal changes to monitor.
  • Council Community Engagement Options for 2026: Staff presented a menu of council engagement methods including chats with council, council-initiated chats, office hours, community connectors updates, and community and council forums. Council members expressed support for chats and forums, nominated a downtown bicycle security walk, and asked staff to return with estimated capacity for each method. The council engagement committee will refine the plan.

entry.title: Boulder: February 5, 2026 Regular City Council Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Parks & recreation, Housing, Zoning, Regional & state relations, Council governance, Budget

  • South Boulder Recreation Center Future and Open Comment: Numerous residents spoke during open comment urging the city to keep the core amenities of the South Boulder Recreation Center, including the lap pool, gym, and weight rooms, citing swim teams, seniors, youth, and accessibility. Speakers also raised concerns about funding priorities relative to office buildings and the East Boulder project. Staff responded that the city has not decided to close a facility, that a $2 million investment was approved in 2025, and that the long-term financial strategy and recreation discussions will return to council in March and May.
  • Black History Month Declaration: Council member Adams presented a declaration recognizing February 2026 as Black History Month, highlighting Boulder's Black community history including early entrepreneurs, the Boulder Blues baseball team, and Second Baptist Church. Representatives from the Black Women's Alliance at CU Boulder and the Black Student Alliance spoke in response.
  • Consent Agenda: Council approved consent agenda items 4A through 4C unanimously, with no discussion raised on the items.
  • Callup Check-ins for Landmark Certificates: Staff presented two landmark alteration certificates in the Mapleton Hill Historic District, one to demolish and rebuild an accessory building at 2408 street and one to construct a new primary building at 2439 Broadway. No council members called either item up, so both proceeded without further review.
  • Rezoning of 5501 and 5505 Arapahoe Avenue to MU-4: Council held a second reading and public hearing on ordinances rezoning approximately 2.65 acres at 5501 and 5505 Arapahoe Avenue from BC-1 to MU-4, plus adjacent right-of-way. Staff noted the change aligns with the East Boulder subcommunity plan and mixed-use transit-oriented designation, and the associated form-based code review was previously approved. One speaker opposed increased density, and both ordinances were adopted unanimously.
  • 2026 Policy Statement on Regional, State, and Federal Issues: Staff presented recommended additions to the 2026 policy statement from the intergovernmental affairs committee, including human rights language, support for federally funded research jobs, food supply and local grower support, orphaned well cleanup, workforce housing, construction defects reform, coal ash mitigation, wildfire guidance, protections against surveillance, and data center water and energy conservation. Council members affirmed existing electrification positions and raised questions about how excessive resource use would be determined.
  • House Bill 26-1010 (HOME Act) Discussion: Staff summarized state House Bill 26-1010, which would allow residential development on qualifying nonprofit, school, church, university, and transit-owned parcels of five acres or less through administrative approval in any zone. Staff outlined permitted local standards, prohibited restrictions on height and unit counts, and political context, noting the bill is a governor's priority. Council members raised concerns about loss of home rule, lack of affordability requirements, nonprofit definitions, and compatibility with the comprehensive plan. After a straw poll, council chose to pursue amendments, including tying projects to demonstrated needs, excluding unincorporated county land, tightening nonprofit eligibility, applying height standards consistent with the zone, limiting project size, and requiring comprehensive plan compatibility.
  • Council Retreat Follow-up on Priorities and Process Improvements: Staff presented scoping for council priorities including bicycle security and theft reduction, wildfire home hardening and assessment, a tip credit ordinance exploration, power resiliency with Xcel Energy, and sister city program updates. Process improvements discussed included board packet timing, CAC request tracking, historic designation presentations, and limiting late meetings. Council members asked that the Title 9 rewrite be recorded as a conditional priority and requested clarity on ebike regulations, climate and agriculture work, and public safety updates.

entry.title: Boulder: January 22, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Economic development, Zoning, Development projects, Taxes & fees, Council governance, Wildfire

  • Opening, announcements, and roll call: The meeting was called to order with an announcement about 2026 boards and commissions recruitment, which is open until January 25th. Council took roll call and confirmed a quorum was present.
  • International Holocaust Remembrance Day declaration: Mayor Pro Tem Winer read a declaration recognizing January 27th, 2026 as International Holocaust Remembrance Day. The declaration condemns antisemitism, hatred, and bigotry and pledges solidarity with the Jewish community.
  • Consent agenda items 3A through 3G: Council discussed the consent agenda, including a letter to Xcel Energy regarding expectations after the city declined an offer in 2025. Council praised staff's draft and then passed items 3A through 3G unanimously.
  • Ordinance 8731 purchasing procedures update: Staff presented updates to the city's purchasing code, the first since 1997, including raising the informal bid threshold from $50,000 to $100,000, allowing alternative construction delivery methods, and creating a business opportunity program. Council asked about support for small, minority, and women-owned businesses and about environmental sustainability language. Ordinance 8731 was adopted unanimously after a public comment period.
  • Community change requests for the Boulder Valley Comprehensive Plan update: Staff screened 34 community change requests for the comprehensive plan update and recommended which should advance for further analysis. Council removed request 10 on the south side of Sue Drive after residents raised concerns about lack of outreach and neighborhood impacts, and added back requests 26 and 27 on wildfire mitigation and agricultural water use. Council approved the amended list unanimously.
  • Metro district policy framework: Staff presented a policy framework for regulating commercial-focused metropolitan districts, covering development type, mill levy caps, operations and maintenance, fees and revenue bonds, privately placed debt, and amendment oversight. Council asked questions about governance, oversight, and competitiveness and generally supported the approach. Staff plans to return in April with a regulating ordinance and model service plan.
  • Regional homelessness working group appointment: Council discussed filling a vacancy on the Boulder County Elected Officials Regional Working Group on Homelessness, previously held by Lauren Folkart. Council members Matt and Mark were asked to resolve who would volunteer, with Tina volunteering as alternate, and the appointment will be handled later on consent.

entry.title: Boulder: January 8, 2026 City of Boulder City Council Special Meeting
entry.content:
Most discussed: Public comment, Council governance, Climate & sustainability, Water & flooding, Development projects, Zoning

  • Agenda Amendment and Public Comment Period: Council unanimously amended the agenda to add an item on the city's response to the power shutoff and windstorms and to remove a proposed letter to Xcel Energy, which will return January 22. Speakers during open comment raised issues including surface parking and a car-free redesign near Mesa Laboratory, Flock Safety camera risks and data misuse, CU student move-out and wildlife eco-visits, Xcel and divestment, proportional representation, Palestinian-related concerns, Boulder recreation center plans, and homelessness sweeps. Staff responded to questions about community resilience hubs and closed captioning, and Council discussed data protection policy.
  • Power Shutoff and Windstorm Response Report: Staff reported on the city's response to the December public safety power shutoff and high-wind event, noting that about 60 percent of the community lost power. Fire, police, utilities, parks, housing, and communications teams coordinated through the emergency operations center, with fire call volume more than doubling. Staff announced a virtual community town hall and an after-action review, and coordination with the Office of Disaster Management and the Public Utilities Commission on Xcel PSPS practices. Council thanked staff for their work.
  • Consent Agenda: Council approved the consent agenda items 4A through 4C and 4E through 4K unanimously, with item 4D removed. Item 4G approved a governing agreement with the Sundance Institute to host the Sundance Film Festival in Boulder from 2027 through 2036. Council members raised concerns about community benefit tracking, the lack of an equity analysis, and the need for annual reporting on the parking revenue share.
  • Downtown Commercial District Board Actions: The council convened as the Downtown Commercial District Board of Directors and unanimously approved Resolution 319, which approves incentives for the Sundance Institute and authorizes the general manager to negotiate and execute a lease. Parking revenue sharing covers up to 1,000 spaces during the festival at a 50/50 split, and staff will compile annual incentive statistics.
  • Call-Up of 5501 and 5505 Arapahoe Avenue Form-Based Code Review: Council considered calling up a five-story mixed-use project with 300 dwelling units and retail space at 5501 and 5505 Arapahoe Avenue, reviewed under form-based code, after the Planning Board raised concerns about aesthetics and mass. Council members argued that the project followed the adopted code and that aesthetic concerns should be addressed through code changes rather than discretionary call-ups. The motion to call up the project failed on a 4-5 vote.
  • Nwood Metropolitan District 2025 Budget Amendment: Council convened as the Nwood Metropolitan District Board and approved Resolution 4, a supplemental 2025 budget appropriation of about $7,400 to cover higher-than-expected dissolution and administrative expenses. Staff noted an accounting error from the prior year that produced a negative fund balance, with suppliers agreeing to delay payment. A public comment period was held, with one speaker raising budget concerns, and the resolution passed unanimously.
  • Annexation and Initial Zoning of 915 Fifth Street: Council held the second reading and public hearing on a series annexation of 915 Fifth Street, about 1.294 acres, with initial Residential Estate zoning. Staff recommended approval without the Planning Board's proposed 4,000-square-foot floor area limit, noting existing zoning standards and topography already restrict development and that the applicant opposed the limit. Council unanimously adopted Resolutions 1364 and 1365 and Ordinances 8728, 8729, and 8730, which includes consent to inclusion in the Northern Colorado Water Conservancy District.
  • Wildfire Hardening and Water-Wise Landscaping Ordinance 8721: Council considered the continued second reading of Ordinance 8721, which updates landscaping, water conservation, and wildfire resilience rules, including moving technical standards into a city landscape manual and addressing state nonfunctional turf requirements. Staff revised the proposal to drop tree removal requirements, require limbing up trees in the wildland-urban interface, limit daytime watering restrictions to summer, and ease other rules, while keeping non-combustible zones near structures. Council praised the flexibility and community engagement and unanimously passed the ordinance with amendments for third reading.
  • 2026 Council Committee and Board Appointments: Staff walked council through vacant seats on boards, committees, and sister city liaison roles, asking members to indicate interest. Members volunteered for the Boulder County Consortium of Cities, Mile High Flood District, Charter Committee, Financial Strategy Committee, and other roles, and several members swapped sister city assignments. Council discussed staggering terms on the Financial Strategy Committee and clarifying whether a homelessness working group appointment still needed to be filled.
  • Closing Comments: Council members thanked staff for responsive work on heating complaints and raised concerns about affordability of water for tree watering during winter, which staff said was addressed in a utilities blog post and resident correspondence. The meeting was adjourned at 8:24 p.m.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Study Session - October 12, 2023
entry.content:
Most discussed: Parking, Zoning, Open space, Development projects, Transit, Council governance

  • Opening remarks and Israel-related statement by Council Member Tara Winer: Council Member Tara Winer, speaking in her individual capacity, expressed heartbreak over the October 7 Hamas attacks in southern Israel, including on Boulder's sister city Ramat Hanegev. She described Boulder's ties to the region through sister city and SIP (Sustainable Israeli Palestinian projects) work and called for peace in the Middle East. Council Member Aaron Brockett noted he had emailed the mayor of Ramat Hanegev expressing personal and city support.
  • Camp shiaka access management plan evaluation and recommendations: Staff from Community Vitality, Transportation and Mobility, and Open Space and Mountain Parks presented an evaluation of the Camp shiaka parking and shuttle program, which has run since 2017 and whose ordinance sunsets at year end. Staff recommended continuing the Camp season with planned changes such as micromobility access, a permanent B-cycle station, signage updates, and routing changes, and possible modifications including performance-based pricing, a commuter permit program, and using parking revenue for transportation demand benefits. Staff also recommended a feasibility study for direct transit or microtransit access beyond the park-and-ride model. Council generally supported continuing the program and the feasibility study, with concern about fairness to Boulder residents who cannot easily access the park and about raising parking costs.
  • East Boulder subcommunity plan zoning and form-based code implementation update: Planner Kathleen King presented the next phase of implementing the East Boulder subcommunity plan, including a zoning study for areas of change and an evaluation of whether form-based code should apply. Staff reviewed feedback from the technical advisory committee, focus groups, and planning board on the existing form-based code in Boulder Junction and Alpine Balsam. Challenges raised included creative limits, commercial affordability, added cost from discretionary call-ups, and limited family-friendly outdoor space. Council members asked for less discretionary review, a more selective set of rules, more roof-form variety, and flexibility for iconic buildings. Staff will return in a few months with draft recommendations.
  • Council discussion on supporting Boulder County Ballot Measure 1A: Council discussed whether to support Boulder County Ballot Measure 1A, a 0.5% sales tax extension for open space purchase and maintenance. Council Member Aaron Brockett noted that a separate letter of support for measure 1B had already been sent. Council members indicated unanimous support for taking a support position, and staff was asked to place the item on consent at the next business meeting.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Regular Meeting - Thursday October 5, 2023
entry.content:
Most discussed: Budget, Taxes & fees, Homelessness, Transportation, Council governance, Affordable housing

  • Call to order, agenda amendment, and proclamations: Mayor Brockett called the meeting to order and roll call was taken. Council unanimously amended the agenda to add a National Domestic Violence Month declaration and a notice of intent for safe outdoor spaces. Council adopted an Indigenous Peoples' Day declaration for October 9, 2023 and the National Domestic Violence Month declaration.
  • Open comment on reservoir fees and rowing access: Several rowing club members and parents, including University of Colorado and Colorado Junior Crew representatives, asked council to reduce after-hours reservoir fees, restore earlier opening hours, and keep non-motorized sports affordable. Staff responded that water quality, staffing, and cost recovery drive the fee structure and that adult users must pay full costs.
  • Open comment on pollinator gardens, lighting, and street safety: Residents spoke about native pollinator gardens in transportation projects, lighting on the Boulder Creek path between 30th and Foothills Parkway, a four-way stop request at 23rd and Bluff Street, and bike lane conditions on Foothills Parkway. Staff committed to following up on lighting and transportation concerns.
  • Open comment on policing, historic preservation, and homelessness: Residents raised concerns about a deputy chief's past conduct in Aurora, the Civic Center historic district application, sale of city buildings, and a proposed drug treatment facility. Other speakers urged support for unhoused residents, including tiny homes and shelter alternatives, and criticized the city's encampment enforcement approach.
  • Staff response to open comment and consent agenda: Staff responded to comments on transportation, the stolen-property complaint, the Aurora-related police matter, and reservoir fees. Council passed consent agenda items 3A through 3G unanimously, with the mayor pro tem voting no on item 3G. Items included a Boulder Creek pollinator item, a police oversight ordinance, and council employee evaluation process.
  • Prairie dog management on irrigated agricultural lands: Open Space staff reported on a three-year review of the prairie dog management program on irrigated agricultural lands. Staff found the program is working, with over 457 acres of prairie dogs removed and 72 acres restored. Staff proposed expanding removal and limited burrow disturbance systemwide to irrigable transition and removal areas.
  • Annexation of property at 3033 Third Street with RL-1 zoning: Council held a public hearing and adopted Resolution 1333 and Ordinance 8582 annexing approximately 0.27 acres at 3033 Third Street with an initial zoning of RL-1. The annexation includes an area 3 preservation term and inclusionary housing requirements. Planning Board recommended approval.
  • 2024 budget public hearing and council proposed changes: Staff presented the recommended 2024 budget of about $14.8 million across all funds and a general fund of $16.1 million. Council discussed proposed changes including community connectors funding, ambassador program funding through CID, pavement management, underpass lighting, and reallocation of Safe and Managed Public Spaces funds. Council adopted Ordinances 8595, 8596, 8597, and 8598 with amended transportation and general fund appropriations.
  • Public hearing testimony on budget priorities: Speakers urged council to fund affordable homeownership protections, mental health support for young adults with autism, nonprofit family homelessness prevention (Keep Families Housed), culturally appropriate mental health care, and community connector compensation. Other speakers raised rent and HOA cost concerns and asked for transit and bike safety investments.
  • Safe outdoor space pilot notice of intent: Council gave direction, by a majority, for staff to develop a pilot safe outdoor space for approximately 25 people, with basic infrastructure and services, and a possible safe outdoor parking component. Staff will return with cost, location, and implementation details. The notice of intent was approved by majority vote after discussion of funding sources and metrics.
  • Council updates and future agenda items: Council member Matt Benjamin announced he will chair the Colorado Municipal League policy committee from October through March. Council member Rachel Friend requested a future conversation on bike safety, including e-bike conflicts on paths. Council adjourned at 10:51 p.m.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Meeting, September 28, 2023 (Study Session: Municipal Court update, Police Department update, and Homelessness programs update)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Homelessness, Crime & justice, Zoning, Budget, Police, Public health

  • Municipal Court operations and philosophy: Judge Khan presented the Municipal Court's problem-solving approach, administrative and staffing changes, and the state-mandated livestreaming of proceedings. He described the FastTrack process for student quality-of-life violations, which aims to see defendants within days and emphasizes restorative justice. Council members asked about the criteria for Community Court and the use of jail sentences, and staff agreed to follow up with more detail at a later date.
  • Jail capacity, bond rules, and the Community Court model: Judge Khan explained the 48-hour rule, personal recognizance bonds, and Boulder County Jail booking standards that limit Municipal Court warrant enforcement. He described the charge-driven prosecution approach and the Community Court model that connects defendants with housing and services. Council discussed frustration with repeat offenders, jail overcrowding, and the need for treatment capacity.
  • Police department crime trends and problem locations: Chief Harold presented five years of crime data showing rising violent crime driven by assaults and menacing, and rising property crime driven by theft, with motor vehicle theft down 48% since 2020. Drug and narcotics violations rose 79% year over year, with overdoses concentrated in downtown and University Hill. Deputy Chief Redfern reported progress at the library and Circle K problem locations.
  • Significant incidents and department highlights: Staff reviewed several recent serious incidents, including an officer-involved shooting, a child homicide, a stabbing outside the municipal building, a Central Park drug operation, and a violent roommate homicide. Staff also highlighted community engagement events, a Spanish-language dinner, the explosives-detection dog, and recognition for women in policing. Council asked about the impact of released defendants and the safety of the community.
  • Homelessness programs and system coordination: Housing and Human Services presented the summer point-in-time count, which showed stable unsheltered numbers, and described new programs including local vouchers, Building Home, the Rest Fit Center, Tribe recovery housing, the high utilizer initiative, and the Day Services Center. Staff reviewed funding braiding, shelter capacity and winter weather plans, and housing exit trends. Council asked about costs, outcomes, and the role of coordinated services.
  • Alternative sheltering and safe outdoor spaces: Staff explored safe outdoor spaces and alternative sheltering models such as pallet shelters, outlining the features that successful programs share and preliminary cost estimates. Council members expressed differing views on safe outdoor spaces versus additional indoor shelter beds and raised questions about funding sources and infrastructure needs. Council directed staff to return with a formal item, likely tied to budget discussions.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Regular Meeting - September 21, 2023
entry.content:
Most discussed: Housing, Affordable housing, Zoning, Development projects, Parking, Council governance

  • Hispanic Heritage Month and Energy Efficiency Day Declarations: Council presented a Hispanic Heritage Month declaration, with Spanish interpretation and remarks from community interpreters and advocates on language justice. Council then presented an Energy Efficiency Day declaration, highlighting energy efficiency's economic and climate benefits and designating October 2023 as Energy Efficiency Day.
  • Open Comment Period: Eight in-person speakers and one virtual speaker addressed council on topics including a library building disposition, a Black history museum exhibit, a homeless camping incident near Central Park, a child-friendly restroom request, a police incident at a hardware store, historic house demolition review, and the 28th and J middle-income housing project. Staff responded on the Central Park incident and child-friendly cities initiative, and council members commented on the library buildings and public safety.
  • Consent Agenda and Call-Up Check-In: Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3F unanimously by roll call vote. For the call-up check-in on a Life Sciences facility at Walnut Street, a council member expressed interest in calling it up for its sustainability leadership, but no member called it up.
  • Boulder Junction Phase 2 Transit Village Area Plan Amendments: Staff presented amendments to the Transit Village Area Plan phase two covering land use categories (mutod, mui, pkuo), urban design, and transportation connections, along with a chapter five summary update. Staff noted market analysis favoring residential uses and the need for business stabilization strategies. Planning board recommended approval with a revision removing office from the neighborhood Tod place type, which staff did not support. Council approved both motions unanimously by roll call vote.
  • Affordable and Modest Size Housing Zoning Ordinance 8599: Staff presented an ordinance amending land use code provisions on site review, density, parking, and subdivision standards to encourage affordable, middle, and modest-sized housing. Changes included exempting certain middle housing from site review, replacing unit-based density with floor area ratios, reducing parking requirements, and allowing duplexes and triplexes in some low-density zones. Council discussed numerous amendments, deferred several to a future phase two, and approved the ordinance on second reading with changes unanimously, with third reading to follow on consent.
  • Letter Supporting County Affordable Housing Ballot Measure: Council member Benjamin proposed a letter to County Commissioners endorsing a proposed affordable and attainable housing tax ballot measure and requesting support for permanent supportive housing with substantial wraparound services and transitional housing. Council agreed to send the letter, with formal endorsement to be considered later through a hotline request.

entry.title: Boulder: September 14, 2023 - Boulder City Council Study Session: Library District IGA Direction and 2024 Recommended Budget Discussion
entry.content:
Most discussed: Budget, Regional & state relations, Council governance, Arts, culture & libraries, Public health, Transportation

  • Library District Intergovernmental Agreement and Board Appointment Process: Staff briefed council on separating the municipal library from the city and transferring assets to the new Library District. Council gave direction to continue a hybrid trustee appointment process with a three-year check-in. Council also agreed to explore long-term leases for library buildings with a district-held termination option at five-year intervals.
  • Library Property Disposition Options: Staff presented options for conveying or leasing city-owned library buildings and land, including Main Library, North Boulder, Carnegie, and Reynolds branches. Straw polls favored leasing the properties rather than conveying them. Council discussed lease length, reversionary interests, maintenance responsibilities, and natural disaster risk.
  • Community Connector Budget Engagement: Community connectors Jamal Gilmore and Lenora Cooper presented findings from seven months of engagement with historically excluded communities. Top priorities included affordable housing, financial security and economic opportunity, and advancing racial equity. Council members thanked them and discussed mental health needs and future partnership.
  • 2024 Recommended Budget Overview: Staff presented the 2024 recommended budget of about $514.8 million, with a general fund of $196.1 million. Key themes included behavioral health response, affordable housing investments, wildfire resilience, employee compensation, and a six-year capital plan of over $900 million. Staff noted revenue constraints, including a potential sales tax expiration and property tax ballot measure.
  • Public Safety, Homelessness and Behavioral Health Investments: The budget includes funding for the CARE and co-response behavioral health programs, encampment management, and ambassadors and urban park rangers. Staff noted that unspent funds and pilot programs will be reviewed. Council members raised questions about the day services center and whether unspent funds could address urgent winter needs.
  • Capital Improvement Program and Community Culture Resilience and Safety Tax Projects: Staff reviewed the six-year capital plan of about $900 million, highlighting the Western City Campus, East Boulder Community Center renovation, fire station replacements, and Civic Area and Pearl Street Mall projects. Debt service for Western City Campus would increase from $3.6 million to $6.1 million annually.
  • Street Maintenance, Potholes and Snow Removal Concerns: Council members raised concerns about pothole repairs and snow and ice removal, citing safety and staffing constraints. Transportation staff said a community engagement process on snow removal is underway and that contractor and staffing capacity remain the main challenges.
  • Budget Review Process and Next Steps: Council was asked to submit proposed budget changes by September 25 so staff can prepare the packet. The first reading is scheduled for October 5, with adoption planned two weeks later. Council members discussed the zero-sum nature of budget changes and the need to identify funding sources.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Meeting - September 7, 2023 (Regular Meeting)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Police, Budget, Council governance, Public comment, Equity & civil rights, Affordable housing

  • Opening Announcements and Agenda Amendment: Council heard announcements about the What's Up Boulder community event and the Better Public Meetings Project scorecard. Council then unanimously voted to amend the agenda, moving item 6B on the Boulder Public Library District intergovernmental agreement to the September 14 study session.
  • Commemorative Declarations: Council read declarations marking the 10th anniversary of the September 2013 Front Range flood, National Voter Registration Day, and National Suicide Prevention Month. Jenna Card of Rise Against Suicide spoke briefly in response to the suicide prevention declaration.
  • Open Comment Period: Community Engagement Manager Ryan Hansen reviewed civility and decorum rules for public participation. Eight speakers signed up, and residents addressed topics including a proposed closure of Boulder Municipal Airport, police accountability and a lawsuit, minimum wage and arts funding, Hill commercial area liquor regulations, bear-trash conflicts, South Boulder neighborhood conditions, and homeless camp proposals.
  • Consent Agenda and Resolution 1339 on LGBTQ+ Public Accommodations: Council reviewed a call-up item for a site review at 1345 28th Street for 303 student housing units and no member called it up. Council then approved the consent agenda items A through I unanimously, including Resolution 1339 supporting LGBTQ+ people's access to goods and services without discrimination following the 303 Creative v. Elenis decision.
  • Reimagining Policing Plan Acceptance: Chief Maris Harold presented the Reimagining Policing Plan, a visionary blueprint developed over roughly two years with community engagement, National Policing Institute research, and a process subcommittee. Deputy Chief Redfern outlined problem-solving policing, staffing based on the rule of 60, and accountability metrics, while the City Manager noted that funding requests would return through the budget process. Council unanimously accepted the plan and disbanded the process subcommittee after extensive public comment, both supportive and critical.
  • Inclusionary Housing Program Update: Staff and consultant Kaiser Martin Associates presented options to update the Inclusionary Housing program, including switching cash-in-lieu to a per-square-foot basis, reducing the on-site for-sale requirement from 25% to 15%, and exploring a nexus study for a linkage fee on demolitions and large additions. Council gave feedback that most members supported the cash-in-lieu and code cleanup changes but were split on the middle-income on-site trade-off, and asked staff to strengthen incentives for on-site units. No formal action was taken, and second reading is targeted for November 2.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Study Session 8-24-23 (Community Broadband, Airport Community Conversation, Minimum Wage)
entry.content:
Most discussed: Labor & wages, Economic development, Regional & state relations, Transportation, Technology & broadband, Arts, culture & libraries

  • Community Broadband Update and Path Forward: Staff presented research on internet access, resident survey results, and three potential paths for community broadband: a municipal internet utility, a public-private partnership, or a backbone lease and right-of-way agreement with a private provider. Financial modeling estimated about $218 million in build costs and a required average annual general fund subsidy of about $14 million. Council discussed concerns about cost, competition, shallow trenching impacts, and lease terms, and was generally leaning toward the backbone lease option.
  • Airport Community Conversation Update: Staff presented the Boulder Municipal Airport community engagement process, including open houses, questionnaires, and a community working group that developed four long-term scenarios and near-term action items. Staff noted FAA grant assurances constrain closure options. Council asked about noise, leaded fuel, airspace, and whether further engagement should wait until new Council members take office.
  • Minimum Wage Regional Effort and Timeline: Staff reviewed the regional minimum wage working group with Longmont, Louisville, Lafayette, and Erie, and Boulder County's decision to pursue a faster 2024 implementation. Staff explained the trade-offs of joining the county's timeline, including loss of collaboration and limited engagement. Council debated whether to move to a 2024 increase or hold to the 2025 timeline previously chosen, and ultimately gave a split direction to stay the course.

entry.title: Boulder: Boulder City Council Regular Meeting - Thursday August 17 2023
entry.content:
Most discussed: Housing, Zoning, Public comment, Equity & civil rights, Council governance, Labor & wages

  • Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and Audit Presentation: Audit subcommittee member David Gross presented the 2022 Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and the auditor Clifton Larson Allen's clean opinion, the first time in 33 consecutive years with a GFOA certificate of achievement. The audit found no deficiencies or material weaknesses. The subcommittee unanimously recommended council approve and accept the report. Council members thanked the audit committee and financial staff.
  • Open Comment on Minimum Wage and Community Concerns: Residents spoke during open comment, with many urging council to raise the local minimum wage to at least 15.70 by January 2024 rather than waiting until 2025. Speakers from labor unions, immigrant advocacy groups and the Boulder Area Labor Council cited rising costs and worker hardship. Other speakers addressed airport noise from low-flying planes, the Lahaina and Marshall fire concerns, Indigenous voices in civic life, and support for Human Services funding. Staff noted the minimum wage work is being coordinated through a Consortium of cities.
  • Consent Agenda Items A through I: Council approved consent agenda items 3A through 3I unanimously after a motion and second. Item 3H included a disclosure from a council member who had previously worked with the property owners, who felt able to remain impartial. Item 3J was pulled for separate discussion.
  • Ballot Measures on the 0.15 Percent Sales and Use Tax: Council considered three ordinances on the expiring 0.15 percent sales and use tax: 100 percent to arts, 100 percent to the general fund, and a 50-50 compromise split between arts and general fund purposes including Human Services. Staff said the general fund is severely constrained without renewal and the compromise does not require service cuts. Ordinance 8586 (safe zones for kids) and 8587 (charter changes) were adopted unanimously. Ordinance 8588 (100 percent to arts) failed 5-2-4, and ordinance 8591 (50-50 compromise) was approved 6-3 as an emergency measure so it could reach the November ballot.
  • Call-Up Check-In Item 4A: Council reviewed item 4A, a vacation of a 14-foot utility easement at 2950 Hawthorne Avenue, formerly 3320 28th Street, under ADR 2023-00109. No council member expressed interest in calling it up, so it proceeded.
  • Public Hearing and Adoption of Ordinance 8585 on Occupancy Limits: Council held a public hearing on ordinance 8585, which raises the unrelated-person occupancy limit from three or four to five citywide and changes efficiency units to three occupants, with a provision freezing occupancy in non-conforming uses. Staff said the change is one part of a multi-pronged housing strategy and noted that about 13 percent of units have non-conforming occupancy. Dozens of speakers supported the change for affordability, chosen families, students and LGBTQ residents, while others raised concerns about neighborhood impacts, parking, noise, affordability guarantees and the 2021 bedrooms-for-people vote. An amendment to strike the non-conforming provisions failed 3-6. The ordinance was adopted 6-3 on a roll call vote.
